lead: On the eighth day of Christmas the Church keeps the title that says most about both the child and his mother: Mary is the Mother of God. The readings do not argue the point. They place us beside it. Numbers gives the blessing that Israel's priests spoke over the people, asking for God's face and God's peace. The psalm turns that blessing into a prayer for all nations. St Paul, in the earliest words of the New Testament about Jesus' mother, says that God sent his Son “born of a woman”, so that we might become sons and daughters. In Luke the shepherds find the child, Mary keeps everything in her heart, and on the eighth day the child receives his name. The key words are face, name and child. The blessing asked for in the desert now has a face and a name, and he is with his mother.

r.h: The Lord make his face to shine upon you
set: The Book of Numbers opens with Israel still camped at Sinai, being ordered as a people before the march through the desert. Chapters 5 and 6 give various rules for the purity and holiness of the camp, and this short blessing closes them. It is given to Aaron and his sons, the priests, so it was meant to be spoken aloud over the people.

It is among the oldest prayers of the Bible still in use. Two tiny silver amulets, found in 1979 in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem and dated to about 600 BC, carry words of this blessing. They are centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jews still hear it in the synagogue today, and parents in many Jewish homes say it over their children on the eve of the Sabbath.
str: vv. 22–23: God tells Moses to instruct the priests: this is how you shall bless.
vv. 24–26: the blessing, in three lines, each naming the Lord.
v. 27: the meaning: the priests place God's name on the people, and God himself blesses.
¶ In Hebrew the three lines grow: three words, then five, then seven. The blessing widens as it goes, from protection, to God's favour, to peace.
kw: When God blesses in the Bible, he gives life, fruitfulness and well-being. It is an act, not only a kind wish.
The word for guarding a flock or watching over a house. Psalm 121 uses it again and again: “The Lord is your keeper.”
To see someone's face is to have access and favour; a hidden face means distance. A shining face is the look of a person who is glad to see you.
More than the absence of war. It means wholeness, when nothing is missing and everything is in its right place. It is the last word of the blessing.
vv: The Lord bless you and keep you;
The “you” is singular in Hebrew throughout the blessing. It is said over the whole people, and yet each person hears it spoken to himself or herself.
the Lord make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you;

The word “gracious” means mercy that is not earned. The Church hears this verse with the words of St Paul: God has shone in our hearts to give the light of his glory “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).
the Lord lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace.
To lift up one's face toward someone is to look at them with favour. This verse is why the reading suits 1 January, the World Day of Peace: peace is first of all God's gift.
So they shall put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.
The priest speaks, but God blesses. To carry God's name is to belong to him. The Gospel of today ends with another name being given.
ch: The Catechism says that blessing is “a divine and life-giving action, the source of which is the Father” (CCC 1078). It also says that every baptized person is called to be a blessing and to bless (CCC 1669). The Roman Missal uses this text as one of its solemn blessings at the end of Mass. St Francis of Assisi wrote it out in his own hand for Brother Leo, and that small parchment is still kept in Assisi. Luke's Gospel closes with Jesus lifting up his hands and blessing his disciples (Luke 24:50), as the priests of Israel blessed the people. On this day, Mary shows us the face the blessing asked for.

r.h: That your way may be known upon earth
set: Psalm 67 is a short community prayer. Verse 6 mentions a harvest, so many think that it was sung at a harvest thanksgiving. Its first line takes up the blessing of Numbers 6 and turns it into a prayer. “The Lord bless you” becomes “God be gracious to us”. Then comes the surprise: Israel asks for this blessing so that the other nations may come to know God.
str: vv. 1–2: bless us, so that all nations may know your saving power.
v. 4: let the nations rejoice, for you judge them fairly and guide them.
v. 5: the refrain: let all the peoples praise you.
v. 7: the closing prayer: may God bless us, and may the ends of the earth revere him.
¶ The psalm has its centre in v. 4, where the nations sing. The blessing of one people has become good news for all.
kw: Literally “salvation”. It comes from the same root as the name Jesus, which today's Gospel gives.
Level ground, and so fairness: God judges the nations without favouritism.
The “fear of God” of the Bible: awe before him, the opposite of carelessness.
vv: May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us,
The people answer the priest. The words of Numbers are now in their own mouths.
that your way may be known upon earth, your saving power among all nations.
The little word “that” is the heart of the psalm. God's blessing is never given only for those who receive it.
Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth.
God is not only Israel's shepherd. He guides the nations too. Two days from now, the Church will celebrate wise men from the East being guided to Bethlehem.
May God continue to bless us; let all the ends of the earth revere him.
The Hebrew can be read as a statement or as a wish. The NRSV takes it as a prayer, and the Malayalam POC as a statement of what God has done. Both hold true.
ch: At Christmas the Church hears the psalm's hope fulfilled. Mary's child is the saving power of God made known to all peoples, as Simeon will say when he holds him: “my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is the sign and instrument of unity for the whole human race (Lumen Gentium 1). Psalm 67 reminds her of the same thing: she is blessed in order to be a blessing.

r.h: Born of a woman, that we might be children
set: St Paul writes this strong letter to the Christian communities of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey, perhaps in the mid-50s. Some teachers were telling these Gentile believers that they must also take up circumcision and the Law of Moses. Paul answers that they have already become God's children through faith in Christ.

Just before our reading he uses a picture from family life: a young heir, though he will one day own everything, lives under guardians like a slave until the date his father has set (4:1–2). Our reading tells of that date.
str: v. 4: the time is full; God sends his Son, born of a woman, born under the law.
v. 5: the reason: to redeem and to make us children.
v. 6: the proof: the Spirit in our hearts cries “Abba”.
v. 7: the result: no longer a slave, but a child and an heir.
¶ In four verses, God sends his Son and God sends the Spirit of his Son. The Father, the Son and the Spirit are all at work for us, long before the later Creeds spell it out.
kw: Time is pictured as a vessel being filled. The coming of Christ is not an accident of history: God brings the waiting of Israel to its completion.
A way of saying fully human (compare Job 14:1). Paul does not name Mary, and these are the earliest words about her in the New Testament.
A legal term from the Greek and Roman world. An adopted child had the full rights of an heir. We become by grace what the Son is by nature.
The Aramaic word for father, used in the family. Jesus prayed with it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). The first Christians kept this Aramaic word even when they spoke Greek (see also Romans 8:15).
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,
The Son is sent, so he existed before he was born. He is born of a woman, so he is truly one of us. These few words hold together what the Council of Ephesus would later defend.
in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.
“Redeem” is the language of buying someone out of slavery. The Son accepts our condition so that we might share his.
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”
Notice who is crying out: the Spirit himself, within us. Christian prayer begins when the Son's own prayer is heard in our hearts. Paul changes from “you” to “our”, and so includes himself.
So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.
Paul now uses the singular “you”, as Numbers does. He says this to each person. And he says “through God”: being an heir is God's gift, not something we have earned.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its great chapter on Mary with these very verses (Lumen Gentium 52). The Catechism quotes them to explain the whole faith in the Son of God (CCC 422), and reads “the fullness of time” as the moment of the Annunciation (CCC 484). It also takes v. 6 as a text of the joint mission of the Son and the Spirit (CCC 683, 742). St Irenaeus put the exchange in one line: the Word became man so that man might become a son of God (Against Heresies 3, 19; quoted in CCC 460). Mary's motherhood is thus not a private honour. Through her the Son became our brother, and we became God's children.

set: The angel has just told the shepherds about the Saviour and given them a sign: a child in a manger (2:12). Today's Gospel repeats part of the Gospel for the Mass at Dawn on Christmas Day, and adds one verse, the naming on the eighth day. In this way the Octave closes with the circumcision and the name.
Circumcision on the eighth day was the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). A Jewish boy entered his people's covenant on that day.
str: v. 16: the shepherds hurry and find the child.
vv. 17–18: they tell what they were told, and all are amazed.
v. 19: Mary keeps and ponders.
v. 20: the shepherds go back, glorifying God.
v. 21: the eighth day: the circumcision and the name.
¶ Luke sets up a contrast of movement and stillness. People hurry, speak, wonder and go away. In the centre, Mary keeps everything within.
kw: Mary went “with haste” to Elizabeth (1:39), using a related Greek word. Good news makes people move.
To keep something safely, to hold it together. The tense suggests something she went on doing.
Literally “throwing together”: placing one thing beside another to see how they fit. Mary compares what she has seen with what she has been told.
This Greek word, like the Hebrew behind it, can mean both “words” and “things that happened”. Mary keeps both.
The Greek form of Yeshua, which means “the Lord saves” (Matthew 1:21). It is the same name as Joshua.
vv: So they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the child lying in the manger.
The sign the angel gave is plain and poor. God's glory, which shone around the shepherds in the field, is here a child in a feeding trough, with his mother and Joseph beside him.
and all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds told them.
Luke says only that they were amazed. Amazement is not yet faith. Compare the next verse.
But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart.

The word “but” sets her apart from the others. She does not yet understand everything, and Luke will say the same of her again at 2:50–51. Faith, for Mary, was also a long road of pondering. The Council speaks of her “pilgrimage of faith” (Lumen Gentium 58).
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God
They go back to the same sheep and the same fields, but not as the same men. In this they resemble those who go home from Mass.
After eight days had passed, it was time to circumcise the child; and he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
The Son of God enters the covenant of his own people, and for the first time his blood is shed. Mary and Joseph obey the Law, and they also obey the angel: the name is not their choice.
ch: The Council of Ephesus (431) defended the title Theotokos, “God-bearer”, against those who would call Mary mother only of the man Christ. St Cyril of Alexandria explained that this does not mean that divinity began in her, but that the one born of her in the flesh is God the Word (in substance). The Catechism teaches the same: Mary is truly Mother of God, because the one she conceived as man was none other than the Father's eternal Son (CCC 466, 495). St Augustine says that Mary conceived Christ in her mind before she conceived him in her body (in substance), and v. 19 shows us that same inner life. The Catechism adds that Jesus learned to pray from this mother, who “kept in her heart” the great things of God (CCC 2599). On the circumcision it says that it marks his entry into Abraham's descendants and foreshadows Baptism (CCC 527). And of the name it says that it is the one name that contains everything (CCC 2666).

qa: How can God have a mother, when God has no beginning?

Mary did not give the Son his divinity. The Son is eternal. She gave him his human nature. But a mother is mother of a person, not of a nature, and the person she bore is the eternal Son of God. That is why the Church calls her Mother of God (CCC 466, 495). The title guards the truth about Jesus: the child at her breast is truly God. It does not make her a goddess. She is a creature, saved by her Son, and the Church worships God alone.
Paul says only “born of a woman”. Does that speak against the virginal conception?

No. Paul is not discussing the manner of Jesus' conception here. He is saying that the Son truly became human and entered the human story. He neither denies nor describes the virginal conception. Matthew and Luke tell of it clearly (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–38), and the Church has confessed it from her earliest formulas of faith (CCC 496).
Why was the Son of God circumcised?

Because he truly became a son of Israel. By circumcision he entered the covenant of Abraham and accepted life under the Law (CCC 527). Paul says the same in today's second reading: “born under the law”. The Church honours this: her Saviour, his mother and the apostles were Jews, and the Church lives from the root of Israel (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: In the older Roman calendar 1 January was kept as the Circumcision of the Lord. The calendar revised after the Second Vatican Council restored here the ancient Roman memory of the Mother of God. St Paul VI explained that the solemnity honours Mary's part in the mystery of salvation, and that it is also a fitting day to pray for peace (Marialis Cultus 5). He began the World Day of Peace on this day in 1968. Whether Mass today is of obligation depends on the country and diocese. One of the oldest prayers to Mary, “We fly to your protection, O holy Mother of God”, comes from the Greek-speaking Church of the first centuries. Every Hail Mary says it again: “Holy Mary, Mother of God”.
study: The blessing of Numbers ends with peace. Where in my home or my work do I most need God's peace this year, and over whom could I say this blessing?
Psalm 67 asks for blessing “that your way may be known”. What would change if I saw God's gifts to me as meant for others?
Paul says the Spirit cries “Abba” in our hearts. How does it change my prayer to think of it as the Son's prayer within me?
Mary keeps things in her heart, even things she does not yet understand. What have I been given in the past year that I should sit down and ponder?

lead: Today's readings ask one question: who is Jesus? John's letter answers those who deny the Son, and the Baptist, asked who he is himself, points away to someone greater. Both ask us to hold on to what we have heard about Christ. It suits the memorial of two bishops who spent their lives defending that same faith.

r.h: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you
set: Tradition links the First Letter of John with the Apostle; many scholars think of a disciple in his circle, near the end of the first century. Its author does not name himself. A painful split lies behind it: some members have left the community (2:19), and their teaching about Jesus troubled those who remained. The writer does not call them by name. He reminds his readers of what they already know.
str: vv. 22–23: the liar denies the Son, and so loses the Father as well.
vv. 24–25: abide in what you heard from the beginning.
vv. 26–27: the anointing within you teaches you.
v. 28: abide in him, so as to have confidence at his coming.
kw: Only the letters of John use this word in the New Testament (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). Here it is not one future figure, but anyone who denies who Jesus is.
To stay, to make one's home. The NRSV has it six times in vv. 24–28. It is John's word for a faith that lasts.

In the New Testament only here and in 2:20. It links the believer to the “Anointed One”, the meaning of the word Christ. Many understand it as the Spirit, or the word of God received in faith through the Spirit.
vv: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you.
The writer offers nothing new. In a time of confusion, the answer is to go back to the original preaching, the apostolic faith.
the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and so you do not need anyone to teach you.

This does not reject teachers; the author himself is teaching them in this very letter. He is telling them that they need not follow new teachers who offer a higher knowledge, because the Spirit already leads them in the faith they have received.
And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he is revealed we may have confidence
“Confidence” (parrēsia) is the openness of one who can speak freely, like a child with a parent. The word “coming” (parousia) appears only here in the writings of John.
ch: The Second Vatican Council cites this passage when it teaches that the whole body of the faithful, anointed by the Holy One, cannot err in matters of belief when it agrees from the bishops down to the last of the lay faithful (Lumen Gentium 12; compare CCC 91–92). The word “Christian” itself means “anointed” (CCC 1289). St Augustine, preaching on v. 27, says that the sound of his words reaches the ear, but the true teacher is within (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 3).

set: After the great Prologue, John's Gospel begins its story with a question. A delegation comes from Jerusalem to the Baptist. Here “the Jews” does not mean the Jewish people, to whom John the Baptist himself belonged. It means the religious authorities of Jerusalem, who had reason to ask about a new preacher drawing crowds. Theirs was a fair question.
str: vv. 19–21: Who are you? Not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the prophet.
vv. 22–23: Then who? “The voice.”
vv. 24–27: Why do you baptize? One stands among you whom you do not know.
v. 28: the place: Bethany across the Jordan.
kw: A voice carries a message, and then it is gone. John quotes Isaiah 40:3, where the voice announces the Lord's return through the desert.
The prophet like Moses, promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18, whom many hoped for.
The Baptist's story opens with this word (1:19). In this Gospel, his task is to be a witness (1:7).
vv: He confessed and did not deny it, but confessed, “I am not the Messiah.”
The Evangelist speaks of this with solemn words. In this Gospel, the Baptist's “I am not” stands in contrast with the “I am” sayings of Jesus. To confess, for John, is to say who he is not.
I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness,
He gives no title, only a task. His importance lies entirely in the one he announces.
Among you stands one whom you do not know,
Even now, Christ can be near and go unrecognized. This remains a warning for those who know the Scriptures best, and so for us.
I am not worthy to untie the thong of his sandal.
It was the task of a slave. A later Jewish saying holds that a disciple may do all that a slave does for his master, except this. John ranks himself below that.
ch: St Augustine draws out the contrast: John is the voice, and Christ is the Word. The voice passes, and the Word remains (in substance). The Catechism calls John the “voice” of the Consoler who is coming (CCC 719) and the Lord's immediate forerunner (CCC 523). Every preacher, catechist and parent might learn from him how to speak of Christ and then step aside.

qa: Why does John say he is not Elijah, when Jesus says that he is (Matthew 11:14)?

John denies that he is Elijah returned in person, which is what the question means. Jesus is speaking about John's role, and Luke says that he comes “with the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). The two statements answer different questions.
rite: St Basil (died 379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and St Gregory of Nazianzus (died about 390) were friends from their student days in Athens. Gregory later said that they knew only two roads: the one to the church and the one to the schools (Oration 43). Both defended the faith of Nicaea, that the Son is truly God, in the very spirit of today's first reading. Basil also wrote a treatise on the Holy Spirit and founded a great complex to serve the poor and the sick at Caesarea. Gregory, called “the Theologian”, wrote that what Christ did not assume, he did not heal (Letter 101).
study: John's letter tells me to let what I heard from the beginning abide in me. Which basic truth of the faith, once learned, do I need to come back to?
The Baptist knows who he is not. Which false importance should I let go of, so that Christ may be seen?

lead: Epiphany means “manifestation”. Today the child of Bethlehem is shown to those who were not of Israel. Isaiah sees the nations walking toward the light that has risen over Jerusalem, bringing gold and frankincense. The psalm prays for a king to whom far-off rulers bring gifts, and who protects the poor. St Paul names the mystery that was hidden for ages: the Gentiles are fellow heirs. In Matthew, wise men from the East follow a star, ask the Scriptures of Israel the way, and kneel before a child with his mother. The key words are light, nations and homage. It is the feast of all of us who came from far away.

r.h: Arise, shine; for your light has come
set: Many scholars think that Isaiah 56–66 addresses the Jewish community after some of the exiles returned from Babylon, a little after 538 BC. The promises of return had been glorious, but the reality was hard: a ruined city, a poor people and a small rebuilt Temple. Into this discouragement the prophet speaks to Jerusalem as to a woman lying on the ground, and tells her to get up.
The poem pictures a great procession to Zion. Her own scattered children come home, and with them the wealth of foreign peoples.
str: vv. 1–2: the command: arise, for the light has come, while darkness covers the earth.
v. 3: nations and kings come to that light.
vv. 4–5: lift up your eyes: your sons and daughters return, and your heart thrills.
v. 6: camels from Arabia, gold and frankincense, and the praise of the Lord.
¶ Everything turns on the difference between darkness everywhere and light in one place. Jerusalem does not make the light. It falls on her, and that is why the nations come.
kw: Two short commands, in the feminine singular, addressed to the city. They open the poem, as sudden as a shout to someone sleeping.
From a root meaning weight. God's glory is his real and weighty presence, the same word used when the glory filled the tent (Exodus 40:34).
Usually the peoples other than Israel. In this poem they are not enemies but pilgrims.
vv: Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.
The verb “risen” is the one used for the sunrise. God's coming is described as dawn over a sleeping city.
For darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples;
The prophet does not deny the darkness of the world. Compare the darkness of Herod's fear and scheming in today's Gospel.
Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn.
This verse, with Psalm 72, is the source of the Christian custom of picturing the wise men as kings. Matthew does not call them that.
They shall bring gold and frankincense, and shall proclaim the praise of the Lord.
Midian, Ephah and Sheba are peoples of Arabia, famous for caravans and for incense. Note that Isaiah has no myrrh; Matthew's third gift is new, and the Fathers saw meaning in it.
ch: The Roman liturgy has read this chapter on Epiphany for centuries, because Matthew's story seems to echo it, with its light, its nations coming from afar, its gold and frankincense. The Second Vatican Council took its first words from the same image: Christ is the light of nations, and his brightness is reflected on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1). The Church does not shine by her own light. The Catechism recalls a favourite image of the Fathers: the Church is like the moon, all its light reflected from the sun (CCC 748).

r.h: May all kings fall down before him
set: Psalm 72 is a royal psalm, a prayer for the king of Israel, perhaps on the day of his enthronement. Its title links it with Solomon, whose visit from the Queen of Sheba, with camels and gold and spices, is told in 1 Kings 10. It asks for far more than any earthly king ever gave, and so Israel came to read it as a hope for the Messiah. The ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm, the Targum, names the Messiah in its first verse.
str: vv. 1–2: God's own justice given to the king, for the sake of the poor.
vv. 7–8: peace and a rule without limit.
vv. 10–11: distant kings bring gifts and bow down.
vv. 12–13: the reason: he delivers the needy.
¶ The reason in v. 12 is striking. It begins with “For”. The kings bow to this ruler because of how he treats the poor.
kw: The fair judgment and right order that a king was meant to give, above all to those who have no one else to defend them.
Here v. 7 prays that it may abound “until the moon is no more”: the whole well-being of a people.
The person who is dependent, who has to ask. This word comes three times in the Hebrew of vv. 12–13, and God's king is judged by how such a person fares.
vv: Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to a king’s son.
Justice is asked for first, before wealth or victory. It belongs to God and has to be given.
May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
The River is the Euphrates. Zechariah 9:10 uses the same words of the humble king on a donkey.
May the kings of Tarshish and of the isles render him tribute, may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts.
Tarshish lay far to the west across the sea, and Sheba far to the south. The poet is drawing a map of the whole known world.
For he delivers the needy when they call, the poor and those who have no helper.
The child adored today will one day say that whatever is done to the least is done to him (Matthew 25:40).
ch: The Church sings this psalm on Epiphany with the refrain “Every nation on earth will adore you, Lord”, and hears it fulfilled in the Magi. She also hears in it a programme: the kingdom of Christ is one of justice and peace, as the Preface of Christ the King says, and the Church's care for the poor is no side issue. The Catechism says that those oppressed by poverty are “the object of a preferential love” on the part of the Church (CCC 2448). Gifts brought to this king should reach those he protects.

r.h: Fellow heirs, members of the same body
set: The letter speaks in the name of Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles (3:1). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul who drew on his thought, while others hold to Paul's own authorship. The Church receives it as inspired in either case. The Lectionary leaves out the verses in which the writer speaks of his earlier words and his understanding, and goes straight to the heart of the matter.
The preceding chapter has already said that Christ “has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall” (2:14). Our reading names this as the mystery.
str: vv. 2–3a: a task was given to me by grace: the mystery was made known to me.
v. 5: it was hidden before, and has now been revealed by the Spirit.
v. 6: what it is: the Gentiles belong, on equal terms.
¶ The argument is built on “then” and “now”. What was not known in former generations is now open.
kw: Not a puzzle that cannot be solved, but God's plan, once hidden and now revealed. The Latin renders it by both mysterium and sacramentum (CCC 774).
Literally the management of a household. It is the word behind the Church's later phrase “the economy of salvation”, God's ordered plan.
Three Greek words in a row, all beginning with “with”. The middle one, as far as we know, does not appear in Greek before this letter. Perhaps a new word was needed for a new thing.
vv: for surely you have already heard of the commission of God’s grace that was given me for you,
An office in the Church is a grace, and it is given for others.
In former generations this mystery was not made known to humankind, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit:
The promise to bless all nations through Abraham is old (Genesis 12:3). What is new is the manner: not as visitors or second-class guests, but as full members in Christ.
that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
This is the reading's single great sentence. The Gentiles are heirs of a promise that was first given to Israel. They do not replace Israel; they are joined to its inheritance.
ch: St Leo the Great, preaching on Epiphany, prays that the full number of the nations may enter the family of the patriarchs, and the Catechism takes up his words (CCC 528). The Catechism also says that the people descended from Abraham are the root onto which the Gentiles are grafted (CCC 60; Romans 11:17–24). The Council recalls that Christ, by his Cross, reconciled Jews and Gentiles, and that the Church cannot forget the root from which she draws her life (Nostra Aetate 4). Because this mystery is for all, the Church is missionary by her very nature (Ad Gentes 2).

r.h: They knelt down and paid him homage
set: Matthew alone tells this story. Its first readers had just heard the genealogy from Abraham (chapter 1), and the Gospel will end with the risen Lord sending the disciples to “all nations” (28:19). Already in chapter 2, the nations are on the road.

Herod the Great ruled Judea as a client of Rome until his death in 4 BC, so Jesus was probably born a few years before that date. Herod was an able builder and a very fearful ruler. The Jewish historian Josephus tells how he had even his own sons killed.
str: vv. 1–2: the wise men arrive in Jerusalem and ask a question.
vv. 3–6: Herod is troubled; the chief priests and scribes give the answer from Micah.
vv. 7–8: Herod's secret plan.
vv. 9–10: the star again, and great joy.
v. 11: the house, the child, the homage, the gifts.
v. 12: another road.

¶ There are two kinds of kingship in the story. Herod holds power and fears a child. The child holds no power, and men travel far to bow before him. The title “king of the Jews” appears here, and comes back only in the Passion (27:11, 29, 37).
kw: Originally a Persian priestly class, known also for studying the stars and for reading signs. Matthew says nothing of how many came, or that they were kings. These are later traditions, drawn from the three gifts and from Isaiah 60 and Psalm 72.

The Greek can mean “at its rising” (so the NRSV) or “in the East” (so the Malayalam POC, കിഴക്ക്). The same word is used in v. 1 in the plural for “the East”, and both senses are defended by careful scholars.
To kneel or bow to the ground. Matthew uses it three times in this story (vv. 2, 8, 11): twice truthfully and once, by Herod, as a lie. Later people will do the same to Jesus (14:33; 28:9, 17).
Precious gifts of the East. Frankincense was burned in worship, and myrrh was used in perfumes and in preparing the dead (John 19:39).
vv: Where is the child who has been born king of the Jews? For we observed his star at its rising, and have come to pay him homage.

Numbers 24:17 had spoken of a star coming out of Jacob, in the words of Balaam, himself a seer from the East. Nature takes these men part of the way. The last part of the way they will need the Scriptures.
When King Herod heard this, he was frightened, and all Jerusalem with him;

Many read “all Jerusalem” here as the ruling circle around a violent king, whose fear makes others afraid. It is no judgment on the Jewish people. Mary, Joseph and the child are Jews too, and the Magi will find the way by Israel's own Scripture.
In Bethlehem of Judea; for so it has been written by the prophet:
They quote Micah 5:2, with an echo of 2 Samuel 5:2 on shepherding. The Scriptures give the true answer. The Magi need that answer, which shows they do not come by the star alone.
When they saw that the star had stopped, they were overwhelmed with joy.
The Greek piles up words for joy: literally, “they rejoiced with very great joy”. It is the only emotion Matthew gives them.
On entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother; and they knelt down and paid him homage.
Matthew, who has told the story mostly from Joseph's side, here says “Mary his mother”. They find no throne and no palace, and still they kneel.
they left for their own country by another road.
It is a plain fact of the journey, yet the Church has long heard more in it. No one who has truly met Christ goes home by the same road.
ch: The Catechism says that in the Magi, “representatives of the neighboring pagan religions”, the Gospel sees the first-fruits of the nations, and adds that they find Jesus only by turning toward the Jews and receiving from them the messianic promise (CCC 528). St Irenaeus explains the gifts: myrrh because he would die and be buried, gold because he is a king, incense because he is God (in substance, Against Heresies 3, 9). Origen links the Magi with Balaam's prophecy of the star (in substance, Against Celsus 1, 60). St Leo the Great in his Epiphany sermons says that the Magi stand for all the nations (in substance). The Council says that God is not far from those who seek the unknown God in shadows and images (Lumen Gentium 16). The Magi's road began there.

qa: Were there three of them? Were they kings? What were their names?

Matthew says only “wise men”, and he gives no number and no names. The number three comes from the three gifts, and Origen is among the first to mention it. Tertullian says that the East counted such men almost as kings. The names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar come from much later tradition. The Church uses these traditions freely in art and piety, but they are not the Gospel's own statement.
Was the star a real star, a comet, or a miracle?

We cannot say. Since Kepler, people have proposed a conjunction of planets in 7 BC, a comet or a new star, but no explanation is agreed, and an ordinary star does not stop over one house. Matthew is not giving an astronomy lesson. He tells us that God led seekers by the signs they could read, and then by Scripture.
Does the Gospel approve of astrology?

No. The star does not tell them a fate. It brings them to a person, and they kneel to him, not to the star. The Bible elsewhere rejects seeking the future from the stars (Isaiah 47:13; CCC 2116). God meets them where they are, as he meets each of us, and leads them on.
rite: Rome keeps the Epiphany on 6 January, but in India and many other countries it is moved to the Sunday between 2 and 8 January, as this year. In the Roman liturgy, Evening Prayer speaks of three mysteries on this day: the star leading the Magi, the water made wine at Cana and the Baptism in the Jordan. The Roman Missal also provides, after the Gospel, for the solemn announcement of the date of Easter and the moveable feasts of the new year, since the whole year flows from Easter. Most of us in India are descended from nations that came late to Abraham's promise, so this is very much our feast.
study: The Magi were guided first by what they knew best, and then by Scripture. What has God used to lead me toward him, and do I now let Scripture finish the journey?
The chief priests know the verse, but the Gospel does not tell us that they went to Bethlehem. What do I know about Christ that I have not yet acted upon?
Psalm 72 says kings bow because this king delivers the poor. What gift of mine should reach the poor this year?
“By another road.” What has to change in the way I go home from this Mass?

lead: The light of Epiphany now begins its work. John tells his readers to test every spirit by one question: do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Matthew shows that same Jesus settling in “Galilee of the Gentiles”, and a people in darkness sees a great light. Faith has content, and the light has a place on the map.

set: The letter's community has suffered a split, and those who left claimed the Spirit for their teaching. Many scholars think that they played down the real, bodily humanity of Jesus. In this reading John joins two things: the commandment (believe and love), and the discernment of spirits. The whole of the Christian life is summed up in 3:23.
str: 3:22–24: one commandment with two sides: believe in his Son and love one another.
4:1–3: test the spirits: confessing Jesus come in the flesh is the sign.
4:4–6: you belong to God, and the one in you is greater.
kw: The word for testing metal to see if it is genuine. Not every spiritual claim is from God, and testing is a duty, not a lack of faith.
Literally “to say the same”: to speak openly what the Church says about Christ.
“Flesh” here means real human life, with its weakness and its death. The Church has just kept the Word made flesh at Christmas, and the letter tests all else by this.
vv: And this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another,
“Commandment” is in the singular, with two parts. To believe without loving is empty, and to love without believing loses its source.
Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God;
He says this to those he loves. Strong feelings or great eloquence do not prove that something is from God.
every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,
The test concerns a Person and his real body. The Catechism calls belief in the true Incarnation “the distinctive sign of Christian faith”, and quotes this verse (CCC 463).
for the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.
The little community is not told that it is strong. It is told that God who dwells in it is greater.
ch: St Paul gives the same rule: “test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the gifts of the Spirit are to be received with thanks, and that judging their genuineness belongs to those who lead the Church, who are not to quench the Spirit (Lumen Gentium 12). Discernment in the Church is not done alone. It takes place within the faith received from the apostles.

r.h: The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light
set: With the arrest of John the Baptist, Jesus begins. He settles at Capernaum, a lakeside town in Galilee. Matthew sees this as fulfilling Isaiah 9:1–2. Those northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali were among the first to fall to Assyria in the eighth century BC, and many foreigners lived there; hence “Galilee of the Gentiles”. The reading then leaps to Matthew's summary of the ministry (vv. 23–25), which introduces the Sermon on the Mount.
str: vv. 12–16: Jesus moves to Capernaum, and Isaiah's light dawns.
v. 17: the first preaching.
vv. 23–25: teaching, proclaiming, curing, and the crowds from everywhere.
kw: A change of mind and heart, a turning of the whole life. It is the same word and the same message as the Baptist's in 3:2.
Matthew's usual phrase, with “heaven” used in Jewish reverence for the name of God. It means God's own rule, not a place after death only.
So near as to be at the door. In Jesus' own person the kingdom has arrived.
vv: the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light,
The day after the feast of the star, the same light. Isaiah's verse is about a people in defeat and shame. The light comes first to the lands that had suffered longest.
From that time Jesus began to proclaim, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.”
The order matters: the light comes first and then the call. We turn because something has appeared, not so that it may appear.
Jesus went throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom and curing every disease and every sickness among the people.
Matthew repeats this almost word for word at 9:35. Between the two verses he shows Jesus teaching (chapters 5–7) and healing (chapters 8–9).
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 17 when it says that the first work of the grace of the Holy Spirit is conversion (CCC 1989). St Paul VI wrote that Christ, as evangelizer, first of all proclaims a kingdom, and that everything else is “given in addition” (Evangelii Nuntiandi 8). The people in v. 24 bring him the sick from the whole region: the Church's care for the sick has its pattern here.

qa: How can I test the spirits today, with so many voices and preachers?

John's test still holds: what does this voice say about Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man? Then look at the fruit: does it lead to love of others, humility and peace in the Church (Galatians 5:22–23)? Stay close to Scripture, the Creed and the Church's pastors, and ask for help from a confessor or a spiritual guide.
study: John joins believing and loving in one commandment. Which of the two is weaker in me at present?
Galilee was a place of mixed peoples and old wounds, and the light began there. Which dark corner of my life or my town should I bring to Christ first?

lead: John writes the shortest and greatest definition in the Bible: “God is love”. He does not leave it as an idea. God's love was revealed when he sent his Son. Mark shows what that love looks like: Jesus looks at a tired crowd, is moved in his heart, teaches them and feeds them. The Epiphany psalm continues today with its prayer for a king who cares for the poor.

set: The letter has just warned against false spirits (4:1–6). Now it gives the positive side, and for the rest of the chapter love is its single subject. These four verses are among the most loved in the New Testament. They give the reason for all Christian love: it comes from God and begins with God.
str: v. 7: let us love, because love is from God.
v. 8: whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.
v. 9: how this was shown: he sent his only Son.
v. 10: what love is: not ours first, but his.
kw: The New Testament's word for self-giving love. Its meaning here is shown not by a dictionary but by the Cross.
Only-begotten, unique. The same word as in John 1:14, 18 and 3:16.
The means by which sin is taken away and we are reconciled. In the New Testament only here and in 2:2. God does not need to be made kind: he himself sends the Son, because he already loves.
vv: Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.

John does not say that love is God, nor only that God loves. He says that God's very being is love. Only the Letter of John says this in so many words (4:8, 16). The Catechism calls this God's “innermost secret”: he is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (CCC 221).
In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

If we want to know what love is, we are not to start from our own feelings. We start with what God did. Pope Benedict XVI says that because God has loved us first, love is now not a mere command but a response to a gift (Deus Caritas Est 1).
ch: St Augustine preached ten homilies on this letter in Easter week, and it was in the homily on this chapter that he said his famous words: “Love, and do what you will.” He was speaking about correcting others: love may be strict or gentle, but it must always be the root (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 7). They are not a licence for doing as one pleases, but a measure of everything one does.

set: The apostles have returned from their first mission, and Jesus has taken them to a quiet place to rest (6:30–32). The crowd arrives first. This is the only miracle of Jesus' public life told in all four Gospels. Its background is rich: God fed Israel in the desert with manna (Exodus 16), and Elisha fed a hundred men with a few loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44).
str: v. 34: compassion and teaching.
vv. 35–38: the disciples' solution, and Jesus' answer: you give them something to eat.
vv. 39–40: the people sit in groups.
vv. 41–42: taking, blessing, breaking and giving: all eat.
vv. 43–44: twelve baskets over; five thousand men.
kw: From the Greek for one's inner organs: to be moved in the depths. In Mark it describes what Jesus feels first, before he acts.
The same word for “wilderness” as the desert of the Exodus. The Shepherd of Israel is again feeding his people in the desert.

A Jewish host's blessing of God over bread at the start of a meal. The Malayalam POC says “gave thanks”, which is the sense of the prayer. At the Last Supper Mark has this verb over the bread and “giving thanks” (eucharistēsas) over the cup (14:22–23), the word from which “Eucharist” comes.
vv: because they were like sheep without a shepherd;
Moses prayed that Israel might not be so (Numbers 27:17), and Ezekiel 34 promised that God himself would shepherd his people. The first thing Jesus gives them is teaching.
But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.”
Two hundred denarii was about two hundred days' wages (compare Matthew 20:2). The disciples count what they lack. Jesus asks them to count what they have, however small.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people;
The same four verbs return at the Last Supper (Mark 14:22). The disciples' part is to carry it to the people.
ch: The Catechism says that this miracle, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples, prefigures “the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist” (CCC 1335). The Church also sees here that the priest at Mass, and each of us in our charity, hands on what we have received. The groups of hundreds and fifties recall how Moses organized Israel in the desert (Exodus 18:21), and the “green grass” may recall Psalm 23.

qa: Some say that the real miracle was that people shared the food they had hidden. Is that what Mark says?

No. That is a modern suggestion, and the text gives no hint of it. Mark says that five loaves and two fish fed five thousand men and left twelve baskets over, and the Church reads this as a true act of the Lord's power (CCC 1335). Sharing is certainly the fruit of the miracle in our lives, but it does not replace it.
study: The love John speaks of begins with God loving me. Do I try to earn what has already been given?
“You give them something to eat.” What small thing do I have, which I keep because it seems too little, that Jesus is asking me to put in his hands?

lead: John continues where he left off: since God has loved us, we must love one another, and love of that kind drives out fear. Mark shows the disciples in the middle of a real fear, on the sea at night, when Jesus comes to them with the words, “Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.” Both readings teach us that fear gives way when we know who is near.

set: This passage continues directly from the verses read on Tuesday. John now draws the conclusion. God's love cannot be seen as God is seen; but it can be seen where people love one another. And love has a future: it gives courage when one thinks of the day of judgment.
str: vv. 11–12: if God so loved, we ought to love; and in our love the unseen God becomes present.
vv. 13–16: how we know: the Spirit, the witness, the confession, “God is love”.
vv. 17–18: love perfected gives boldness and drives out fear.
kw: To bring something to its goal. John says God's love reaches its goal in us (v. 12).
This title occurs in the New Testament only here and in John 4:42, where the Samaritans say it. Three days after the Epiphany, it could be the motto of the feast.
Here the fear of punishment, the fear of a slave before his master. It is not the same as the reverent “fear of the Lord”, which is a gift of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).
vv: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.
A startling step. We expect the verse to end, “but we see him in Christ” (as John 1:18 does). Instead John says that the invisible God is known where there is love among people.
And we have seen and do testify that the Father has sent his Son as the Savior of the world.
“We have seen”: the letter began with eyewitness (1:1), and the writer comes back to it. Love in this letter is never cut off from the facts about Jesus.
There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear;

One who is loved does not fear a beating. John is not saying that the Christian never feels afraid. He is saying that fear of God's punishment should not be the last word between a child and the Father.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this verse, compares fear to the needle that goes through the cloth and pulls the thread of love after it: the needle goes out, and the thread remains (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 9). The Catechism says that the person who is moved by love no longer stands before God as a slave, in servile fear, or as a mercenary looking for wages, but as a son responding to the love of him who “first loved us” (CCC 1828).

set: This scene comes straight after the feeding of the five thousand, read on Tuesday. Jesus sends the disciples away by boat, dismisses the crowd and goes up the mountain to pray. In the night, a contrary wind holds the boat back on the Sea of Galilee. The disciples, as the Gospel says at the end, have not yet understood what happened with the loaves.
str: vv. 45–46: he sends them on and goes up to pray.
vv. 47–48: he sees them straining, and comes walking on the sea.
vv. 49–50: they are terrified; he speaks.
vv. 51–52: he gets in, the wind stops, and they still do not understand.
kw: A strong word: he compelled them. The Malayalam POC rightly says “നിർബന്ധിച്ചു”. Jesus himself sends them into the night.
The language of God showing himself: God passes by Moses (Exodus 33:19–22; 34:6) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:11).
Literally “I am”. In ordinary Greek it can mean simply “It's me”. But in a scene where someone walks on the sea, as only God does (Job 9:8), the words recall the name of God in Exodus 3:14.
vv: After saying farewell to them, he went up on the mountain to pray.

Mark shows Jesus at prayer alone at only three moments (1:35; 6:46; 14:32–39), each of them a time of decision. The Catechism says that he often went apart to pray in solitude, on a mountain, preferably at night (CCC 2602).
When he saw that they were straining at the oars against an adverse wind, he came towards them early in the morning, walking on the sea.

He sees them from the land, even when they cannot see him. The Greek says “about the fourth watch of the night”, between three and six in the morning, as the Malayalam POC has it. They have rowed all night. His help comes late, but it comes.
But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.”
Three short phrases. Fear is answered not with an explanation but with a Person. The same words, “Do not be afraid”, opened the pontificate of St John Paul II on 22 October 1978.
for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.

Mark does not hide the disciples' slowness. A hard heart here does not mean malice, but dullness. Those who saw the bread multiplied do not yet see who gave it. This is an encouragement to us who are also slow.
ch: An ancient Christian image sees the boat as the Church, tossed about in the world and kept safe by Christ. Tertullian uses it, of the disciples in the boat, in his work On Baptism (in substance). The Church also learns here that the Lord does not always remove the wind at once. He sees, he comes in his own time, and he gets into the boat with us. That is the Epiphany again: the same Lord shown to the wise men is now shown to his own frightened friends.

qa: Why did Jesus intend “to pass them by”? Was he going to leave them?

No. It is not about ignoring them. In the Old Testament, when God “passes by”, he is showing himself to someone (Exodus 33:19–22; 1 Kings 19:11). Mark's words tell us that this is a revelation of God's presence, as much as a rescue.
study: John says that “no one has ever seen God” but that God lives in us if we love. Who might be coming to know God through the way I love?
He made them get into the boat, and the wind came against them. When have I found that doing what the Lord asked did not mean a calm sea?

lead: John closes his long meditation on love with a blunt test: whoever hates a brother or sister cannot claim to love God. Luke brings us to the synagogue at Nazareth, where Jesus reads Isaiah and says, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” God's love, shown to the nations at Epiphany, now has a programme: good news to the poor.

r.h: We love because he first loved us
set: The last part of John's meditation on love ties together everything he has said: love of God, love of others, faith in Jesus and obedience. It moves in a circle. Whoever believes is born of God; whoever is born of God loves him and those born of him; and such love shows itself in keeping the commandments.
str: 4:19: God's love comes first.
4:20–21: the visible brother and the invisible God.
5:1–3: believing, being born of God, loving and obeying are one.
5:4: faith is the victory.
kw: In John it is not only a violent feeling. It also means to refuse love, to close one's heart (compare 3:17).
Literally “heavy”. Jesus says that his burden is light (Matthew 11:30). A commandment does not feel heavy to the one who loves.
This noun comes only here in the New Testament. Compare Jesus' words: “I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).
vv: We love because he first loved us.

A note on the text. Many of the best manuscripts have no object: simply “we love”. Some others add “him” or “God”, and the Malayalam POC follows that sense (അവിടുത്തെ സ്നേഹിക്കുന്നു). Both are true. All our love, for God and for others, is a reply.
for those who do not love a brother or sister whom they have seen, cannot love God whom they have not seen.
One who says he loves God has an easy claim to make, because God is out of sight. The person beside me is not. Love of God can be tested there.
And his commandments are not burdensome,
John does not mean that it is easy, but that it is not a dead weight. It is lifted by the love of the one who commands and by the life he gives.
And this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.
“World” in this letter means life organized without God. The small, wounded community is told that it has already won, through the faith by which it holds to Christ.
ch: Pope Benedict XVI explains that this verse does not set love of God and love of neighbour against each other: love of neighbour is a path to God, and closing our eyes to our neighbour makes us blind to God as well (Deus Caritas Est 16). The Catechism uses v. 20 in teaching the “forgive us” of the Our Father (CCC 2840).

r.h: Today this scripture has been fulfilled
set: Luke places this scene right at the start of Jesus' ministry, and earlier than the visit to his home town in Mark and Matthew (Mark 6:1–6). He uses it as an opening programme for the whole Gospel. Jesus has come through the Baptism and the temptations, and returns “filled with the power of the Spirit”.

The quotation joins Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6. It ends before the words “and the day of vengeance of our God”. Today's reading stops at the admiration of the people; the question about Joseph's son and the conflict follow.
str: vv. 14–15: the return to Galilee and the teaching.
vv. 16–17: Nazareth, the sabbath, the scroll.
vv. 18–19: the text from Isaiah.
vv. 20–21: he sits; all eyes are on him; “Today”.
v. 22a: their amazement.
kw: The verb behind “Christ”. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; this one is anointed by the Spirit himself (compare Acts 10:38).
The word for the release of slaves and the cancelling of debt in the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10, in the Greek), and also the word for “forgiveness” of sins in the rest of the New Testament.
One of Luke's favourite words: “to you is born this day” (2:11), “Today salvation has come” (19:9), “today you will be with me” (23:43). With Jesus, God's promise is no longer only in the future.
vv: When he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, he went to the synagogue on the sabbath day, as was his custom.
He is a faithful Jew who keeps the sabbath and goes to the synagogue, and Luke says that it was his habit. Our own weekly going to Mass has its model here.
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.
This is the first thing that Jesus says about himself in public in Luke. The first people he names are the poor.
The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him.
Luke slows the scene down. He rolls up the scroll, gives it back, and sits, which is the posture of a teacher. Everyone waits.
Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

It is the first sentence of his teaching in Luke, and it is the shortest of homilies. The Scripture is fulfilled not only in his person but “in your hearing”: the moment it is heard is the moment it acts.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ opens his preaching of the Good News by making this passage of Isaiah his own (CCC 714), and that he is sent to the poor (CCC 544). The Second Vatican Council teaches that Christ himself speaks when the holy Scriptures are read in the Church (Sacrosanctum Concilium 7), and so v. 21 is true at every Mass. Origen tells his hearers that they too, in their assembly, can have the eyes of their hearts fixed on the Saviour (in substance, Homilies on Luke 32).

qa: There is someone I cannot love; I still feel hurt and anger. Does this verse mean that I do not love God?

Love is not first a feeling. It is a decision of the will: to wish that person well, to refuse revenge, to pray for him or her. The Catechism says that it is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offence, but that the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion and purifies the memory (CCC 2843). Bringing the hurt to God is already a way of obeying this verse.
rite: Today the Roman calendar allows an optional memorial of St Raymond of Penyafort (died 1275), a Spanish Dominican priest. At the request of Pope Gregory IX he gathered the Church's laws into one great collection, and he wrote a well-known guide for confessors. His life is a reply to anyone who thinks law and love are enemies: in him, as in today's first reading, the commandments serve love.
study: Whom do I see each day, whose presence tests my claim to love God?
Jesus says “Today”. Which line of the Scripture I hear at Mass this week might I let be fulfilled today, in my own hearing and my own life?

lead: The Christmas season is about to close, and both readings ask who this child really is and what he brings. The First Letter of John answers in the language of a court: God himself has testified to his Son, and the verdict is life. In Luke a man covered with leprosy learns the same thing through a hand laid on his skin. The psalm praises the God who “sends out his command to the earth”; in Jesus that word comes close enough to touch.

set: The letter was written for a community that had been through a painful split: some had gone out from it (2:19) and, it seems, denied that Jesus Christ had truly come in the flesh (4:2–3). This passage follows straight on from the reading of 7 January, which ended with the victory of faith, and it draws the letter's argument towards its goal. Many scholars think that its stress on “the water and the blood” answers teachers like Cerinthus, who, as St Irenaeus reports, held that the divine Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and left him before the Passion.
str: vv. 5–8: Jesus Christ came by water and blood; the Spirit, the water and the blood testify together.
vv. 9–12: God's own testimony is greater than any human one: he has given us eternal life in his Son.
v. 13: why the letter was written: so that believers may know that they have eternal life.
kw: A word from the law court. The noun and its verb come again and again in these verses. Faith here does not rest on a feeling but on a witness, and the witness is God.
Probably the baptism of Jesus and his death on the Cross: he is the Son of God not only at the Jordan but on Calvary as well. It also recalls the water and blood from his pierced side (John 19:34).
In John's writings this is not only life after death. It is God's own life, already given to the one who is joined to the Son.
vv: This is the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not with the water only but with the water and the blood.
The repeated “not with the water only” shows the point in dispute. The Passion is no accident that happened to someone else. The Son of God himself went through it.
There are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood, and these three agree.

A note on the text. Older printed Bibles add here a sentence about three witnesses in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit. It is called the “Johannine comma”. It is missing from the early Greek manuscripts and is a later addition known from the Latin tradition, so modern Catholic Bibles, including the NRSV and the POC, do not have it. Faith in the Trinity does not depend on it.
Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
The whole letter in one line. Life is not a reward kept apart from Christ. To have him is to have it.
ch: The Catechism says that the blood and water from the side of the crucified Jesus are types of Baptism and the Eucharist, the sacraments of new life (CCC 1225). So the testimony of 1 John 5 goes on in the Church: at the font and at the altar the Spirit still bears witness to the Son. Verse 13 is close to the purpose given at the end of John's Gospel: “that through believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

set: This comes early in the ministry in Galilee, just after the call of Simon Peter at the lake (5:1–11). According to Leviticus 13–14, a person with a skin disease of this kind had to be examined by a priest and “shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). The rule was there to protect the holiness and health of the community, but for the sick man it meant being cut off from home, worship and touch. Luke does not say that he came to the town illegally. He only says that he saw Jesus and fell on his face.
str: v. 12: the man's prayer.
v. 13: the touch, the word, the healing.
v. 14: the order to keep silent and to go to the priest.
vv. 15–16: the crowds grow, and Jesus withdraws to pray.
kw: Literally “full of leprosy”: Luke alone gives this detail. The biblical word covers various skin diseases, not only what is called leprosy today.
The man says, “if you choose”; Jesus answers with the same verb. The man does not doubt the power. He is asking about the will, and the will is what Jesus gives him first.
Luke's Greek describes a habit: he kept on withdrawing and praying. Prayer in Luke is the steady ground under all the activity.
vv: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
This is one of the most trusting prayers in the Gospels. It makes no demand, and it leaves everything with the Lord.
Then Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said, “I do choose. Be made clean.”

Under the Law, touching such a man made a person unclean. Here it goes the other way: the touch does not make Jesus unclean, it makes the man clean. A word would have been enough, but this man had long gone without a human touch.
But he would withdraw to deserted places and pray.
At the moment of his greatest success Jesus goes away to be with the Father. The crowds do not set the rhythm of his life.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ makes use of signs to heal, including the laying on of hands, and that he not only allows himself to be touched by the sick but makes their miseries his own (CCC 1504–1505). It also notes that Jesus often draws apart to pray in solitude (CCC 2602). The sending to the priest shows respect for the Law: Jesus does not bypass Israel's way of restoring a person to the community, but sends the man back into it.

qa: Why does my old Bible have more words in 1 John 5:7?

Some older translations, made from later Latin and Greek texts, include “the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit” in the verse. The words are not in the early Greek manuscripts, and modern Catholic Bibles leave them out. The Church's faith in the Trinity rests on the whole of Scripture and Tradition, not on this one line.
study: John speaks of a witness that believers have “in their hearts” (5:10). How has God's testimony to his Son become real in your own life?
The man in Luke asked, “if you choose”. Who in your community lives “outside the camp” today, and what would it mean to touch them?

lead: On the last weekday of the Christmas season the First Letter of John comes to its end, and John the Baptist makes one of his last appearances in the Fourth Gospel. The letter speaks of the boldness of those who know they are heard. The Baptist speaks of the joy of one who knows he is not the centre. Both are about the same thing: a life that has found its place because it has found the Son. The psalm sings that “the Lord takes pleasure in his people”.

r.h: This is the boldness we have
set: These are the closing verses of the letter. Verse 13 gave the purpose of the writing, and what follows gathers up some final assurances: God hears us, we can pray for one another, and we know whose we are. The three solemn “we know” sentences of vv. 18–20 sum up the faith of a community that has been shaken by those who left it.
str: vv. 14–15: confidence that God hears prayer.
vv. 16–17: praying for a brother or sister who sins; sin that is mortal and sin that is not.
vv. 18–20: three times “we know”.
v. 21: the last word: keep away from idols.
kw: Originally the citizen's right to speak openly. Here it is the open, trusting speech of a child with the Father. The Catechism calls it “the certainty of being loved” (CCC 2778).
Literally “sin towards death”. John does not define it. In the setting of the letter many scholars think of a deliberate turning away from Christ and the community, as those who left had done.
An image or a false god. It is an abrupt last word, and it stands against “the true God” of the verse before it.
vv: And this is the boldness we have in him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us.
“According to his will” does not make prayer smaller. It is the prayer Jesus taught: your will be done. The one who prays this way is never unheard.
All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that is not mortal.
Sin is never treated as nothing, yet not all sin is the same. There is always room to pray, and God “will give life” through the prayer of a brother or sister (5:16).
He is the true God and eternal life.

The Greek “he” (houtos) could point back to the Father or to Jesus Christ, the name just mentioned. Many Fathers and modern commentators take it as Jesus Christ, which would make this one of the clearest statements of his divinity in the New Testament. Others refer it to the Father. The verse in either case sets the Son wholly within the truth of God.
ch: The Catechism states that the distinction between mortal and venial sin is “already evident in Scripture”, and cites this passage (CCC 1854). Idolatry, it says, consists in divinizing what is not God, and it remains a constant temptation to faith (CCC 2113). So the last verse of the letter is not an old warning about temples alone. Money, power and even the self can be set in God's place.

set: After the night conversation with Nicodemus, Jesus moves into the Judean countryside, and for a time he and John the Baptist are both baptizing. The evangelist later adds that it was not Jesus himself but his disciples who baptized (4:2). The place of Aenon is not known for certain; its name probably comes from a word for springs. The discussion in v. 25 is among fellow Jews about purification, a serious religious matter. It is not an attack on the Jewish people. John's disciples are simply worried that their teacher is losing his following.
str: vv. 22–24: two baptizers at work.
vv. 25–26: the disciples' complaint: “all are going to him.”
vv. 27–28: John's answer: everything is a gift; I am not the Messiah.
vv. 29–30: the friend of the bridegroom and his joy.
kw: The prophets speak of God as the bridegroom of his people (Hosea 2; Isaiah 62:5). By giving this title to Jesus, John says something very great about him.
At a wedding the bridegroom's friend stood by him and helped him. The friend's joy is not to have the bride, but to hear the bridegroom's voice.
“He must increase”. In John this little word often points to God's plan, as in “so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (3:14). John's decreasing is not a defeat. It is part of the plan.
vv: “No one can receive anything except what has been given from heaven.
The cure for envy. If everything is a gift, there is no competition among those who have received.
The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. For this reason my joy has been fulfilled.
His followers bring him bad news, and he answers with joy. One who has waited so long for the bridegroom can only be glad when he comes.
He must increase, but I must decrease.”
These are among the Baptist's last words in this Gospel, and they could stand over any Christian ministry. The one who points to Christ succeeds when people look away from him and towards Christ.
ch: The Catechism says that the Baptist rejoices in being “the friend of the bridegroom” (CCC 523), and that when the Church celebrates his birth and martyrdom she unites herself to his desire: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (CCC 524). St Augustine noticed that the Church keeps John's birth at the time when the days begin to shorten and Christ's at the time when they begin to lengthen, and saw this verse in it (in substance).

qa: What is the sin John tells us he does not ask us to pray about?

John does not name it. Many scholars think he has in mind a settled rejection of Christ, such as that of those who left the community. He says, “I do not say that you should pray about that”; this is not a command against praying. The Church prays for all sinners. The Catechism teaches that there are no limits to the mercy of God, but that one who deliberately refuses to accept his mercy by repenting rejects the forgiveness of sins (CCC 1864). Nobody should conclude that a particular person is beyond prayer.
study: What idols, in the sense of 1 John 5:21, are most tempting in your family or parish?
Think of a work in the Church in which someone else is now given the place you used to have. What would the Baptist's joy look like there?

lead: With this feast the Christmas season ends and the public life of Jesus begins. The child adored in Bethlehem is now a grown man standing in a line at the Jordan, and heaven speaks over him. The readings tell us who he is. Isaiah gives the portrait of a Servant on whom God has put his spirit and who will not break a bruised reed. The psalm hears “the voice of the Lord” over the waters. Peter, in the house of a Roman officer, tells how “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power”. Mark, read in this Year B, gives the event itself in five verses.

One line runs through all four: the Father's voice, the Spirit's coming and the Son's mission. What Isaiah announces in the words “my servant” and “in whom my soul delights”, the voice from heaven applies to Jesus. The key words are servant, anointed and beloved.

set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the Jews exiled in Babylon, in the years before Cyrus let them return (538 BC). Scattered through these chapters are four poems usually called the Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12). Today's reading gives the first of them, and then part of the words that follow it, addressed to the Servant himself.

Who is the Servant? In the verses just before (41:8–9) Israel is called God's servant, and many Jewish and Christian readers have seen the people in this figure; others have thought of a prophet or a coming leader. The New Testament sees the song fulfilled in Jesus: Matthew quotes vv. 1–4 of him (Matthew 12:18–21). The Lectionary leaves out v. 5, a short hymn to God the Creator.
str: v. 1: God presents his Servant: chosen, loved, given the spirit.
vv. 2–3: his way: quiet and gentle with what is weak.
v. 4: his perseverance until justice is established.
vv. 6–7: God speaks to him: called, held by the hand, given as a covenant and a light, to open blind eyes and release prisoners.
¶ The poem says “justice” three times in four verses, and that justice is for the nations and the whole earth, not for Israel alone.
kw: A word for a slave, and also for a king's trusted minister. It is a title of honour in the Old Testament: Moses and David are called the Lord's servants.
Not only a court verdict but the right order of things that God wants among people. The Servant brings it, and he does so without shouting.
The spirit of God comes upon judges, kings and prophets for a task. Here it is “upon him” from the start. The Gospel shows this same Spirit coming down on Jesus.
A striking phrase: the Servant does not merely make a covenant, he is given as one. In his own person he binds God and people together.
vv: Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my spirit upon him;
God's own voice introduces him. These are the words echoed by the voice at the Jordan: “with you I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11).
a bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench;

A reed already bent and a lamp nearly out are the cheapest things in the house. Anyone else would throw them away. His power is shown by what he refuses to destroy. Those who feel nearly finished can take heart from this verse.
I have given you as a covenant to the people, a light to the nations, to open the eyes that are blind,
The mission goes far beyond one nation. Peter's speech in the second reading shows it beginning to come true in the house of a Gentile.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus' baptism is, on his part, the acceptance and inauguration of his mission as God's suffering Servant (CCC 536). The Church therefore reads this song today as the programme of his public life. She reads all four songs in Holy Week, because the gentleness of this first song leads to the Cross. The Servant's opening of blind eyes and release of prisoners is what Jesus actually does in the Gospels.

r.h: The voice of the Lord over the waters
set: Psalm 29 is a hymn to God's majesty in a great storm. The thunder comes in from the Mediterranean, rolls over Lebanon and dies away in the wilderness. Many scholars think it took up the language of older Canaanite hymns and gave all the glory to the Lord alone. The Lectionary uses only the verses at the beginning and end, with the verses on the waters, and the refrain comes from the last verse: the Lord will bless his people with peace.
str: vv. 1–2: the heavenly beings are called to give glory.
vv. 3–4: the voice over the waters.
vv. 9b–10: in the temple all say “Glory!”; the Lord is enthroned as king.
kw: Seven times in the psalm this phrase strikes like a thunderclap. In Hebrew qôl means both “voice” and “thunder”.
Literally “weight”: what is weighty, what counts. The psalm begins and ends the storm with the same word.
Used elsewhere in the Bible only of the great flood in Genesis. The Lord is enthroned above the waters that once threatened all life.
vv: The voice of the Lord is over the waters;
On this feast the verse makes us think of the Jordan: there too the waters are the place where God's voice is heard.
The voice of the Lord is powerful; the voice of the Lord is full of majesty.
and in his temple all say, “Glory!”
The storm is frightening outside, but inside the temple the worshippers have only one word. The same voice that shakes the wilderness now gathers a people in praise.
ch: Christian readers have heard in this psalm the voice of the Father at the Jordan. Thunder becomes a word, and the word is “Beloved”. The refrain turns the psalm's power into a gift: the God whose voice breaks cedars blesses his people with peace, and at Christmas the angels sang of the same peace.

set: This is the turning point of Acts. Cornelius, a Roman centurion at Caesarea who fears God, has been told in a vision to send for Peter. Peter, in his own vision, has been told that he must not call unclean what God has made clean. Now, a Jew in a Gentile's house, he begins to speak. The reading gives the opening of his speech, a short summary of the gospel, with the baptism of Jesus as its starting point.
str: vv. 34–35: what Peter has just understood: God shows no partiality.
v. 36: the message sent first to Israel: peace through Jesus Christ, Lord of all.
vv. 37–38: from the baptism John announced: God anointed Jesus, who went about doing good.
kw: Literally “a receiver of faces”: a judge who decides by looking at who is standing before him. God does not do this.
The phrase echoes Isaiah 52:7, the messenger “who announces peace”. It is the same peace that the psalm's refrain asks for.
From chriō, the root of the title Christos, the Anointed. The Father is the one who anoints, the Spirit is the anointing, and Jesus is the Anointed One.
vv: “I truly understand that God shows no partiality,
It is one of the most moving moments in Acts: after years with the Lord, Peter is still learning. His understanding grows, and it grows because he goes where the Spirit sends him.
but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.
The Second Vatican Council opens its teaching on the People of God with this verse (Lumen Gentium 9). It does not make Christ unnecessary: Peter goes on at once to proclaim him.
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power; how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
A whole ministry in one sentence. The anointing is for action: it leads directly to doing good.
ch: The Catechism explains the title “Christ” with this verse: Jesus is the Christ, for “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” (CCC 453). Baptized Christians share in this anointing: their very name means that they are anointed by the Holy Spirit (CCC 1241).
