r.h: You are my Son, the Beloved
set: Mark has no story of the birth of Jesus. His Gospel begins with “the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1), moves at once to John in the wilderness, and within nine verses Jesus is in the Jordan. Mark tells the scene very briefly, and as something Jesus himself sees and hears: the voice speaks to him directly.
str: vv. 7–8: John points to the stronger one, who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.
v. 9: Jesus comes from Nazareth and is baptized.
v. 10: the heavens torn open; the Spirit comes down.
v. 11: the voice from heaven.
¶ In this short scene the Father speaks, the Son is addressed and the Spirit descends.
kw: To dip or plunge. John's rite was a sign of repentance in the flowing water. Jesus goes into the same water as the sinners who came to it.

A stronger word than “open”. Isaiah had prayed, “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). Mark uses this verb once more, for the temple curtain torn at the death of Jesus (15:38), just before the centurion calls him God's Son (15:39).
The Greek Old Testament uses it for Isaac, Abraham's “beloved” son (Genesis 22:2). So there is already a shadow of sacrifice over this moment.

The word recalls the Servant “in whom my soul delights”. The voice joins two texts: “You are my Son” (Psalm 2:7), spoken to a king, and Isaiah 42:1, spoken of a Servant. Jesus is king and Servant together.
vv: “The one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the thong of his sandals.
Untying sandals was the work of a slave. The greatest prophet of his time says he is unworthy even of that.
In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
Nazareth was a village nobody expected anything from. He comes without a title and without any ceremony. Mark does not even explain why he came; he simply goes down into the water.
And just as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens torn apart and the Spirit descending like a dove on him.
The Catechism sets this dove beside the one Noah sent out at the end of the Flood, the sign that the earth could be lived on again (CCC 701). Heaven, closed for so long, is open.
And a voice came from heaven, “You are my Son, the Beloved; with you I am well pleased.”
Jesus has as yet done nothing in public. Before any miracle or sermon, the Father's love is simply declared. This is the ground on which every Christian life stands as well.
ch: The Catechism sees the whole mystery here. Jesus' baptism is the acceptance of his mission as suffering Servant; he allows himself to be numbered among sinners; the Spirit whom he has possessed in fullness from his conception comes to rest on him, and he will become its source for all humanity; and the heavens that Adam's sin had closed are opened (CCC 536). Through Baptism the Christian is sacramentally assimilated to Jesus, who anticipates his death and Resurrection in his own baptism (CCC 537).

St Ignatius of Antioch wrote that Christ was baptized so that by his suffering he might purify the water (in substance). The Catechism quotes St Gregory of Nazianzus: “Let us be buried with Christ by Baptism to rise with him” (CCC 537), and also St Hilary of Poitiers, for whom what happened to Christ shows what happens to us: the water, the Spirit coming down, and the Father's voice adopting us as sons (in substance).

qa: If Jesus had no sin, why was he baptized?

He did not need it for himself. The Catechism says that he submitted to it voluntarily, though it was intended for sinners, in order to “fulfill all righteousness” (CCC 1224, quoting Matthew 3:15), and that it was a manifestation of his self-emptying. He stands with those he came to save, and in the same act begins the road that leads to the Cross.
Did Jesus become God's Son at his baptism?

No. Some in the early centuries thought so, but the Church rejected the idea. Mark has already called him “the Son of God” in his first verse (the words are in most manuscripts), and the voice declares what is already true. It does not say “you are now” but “you are”. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, as we say in the Creed. What begins at the Jordan is his public mission.
Is John's baptism the same as Christian Baptism?

No. John himself draws the difference: “I have baptized you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Mark 1:8). John's rite was a sign of repentance. Christian Baptism is a sacrament that truly joins a person to the death and Resurrection of Christ, gives the Holy Spirit and makes the baptized a child of God (CCC 1213, 1265).
rite: In the Roman calendar this feast closes Christmas Time, and Ordinary Time begins tomorrow. The Roman liturgy joins the baptism in the Jordan to the mystery of the Epiphany, along with the coming of the Magi and the wedding at Cana (CCC 528): all three show who this child is. Today's Mass prays that those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit may be well pleasing to the Father (in substance). It is a fitting Sunday to bring your family to the baptismal font of your parish, to find out the date of your own Baptism, and to remember that at your Baptism you were anointed with chrism, as a sharer in the anointing of Christ, priest, prophet and king (CCC 1241).
study: The Father says “Beloved” before Jesus has done anything in public. What would change in you if you believed that this was said over you at your Baptism?
Think of a “bruised reed” or a “dimly burning wick” near you. How could you treat them as the Servant does?
Peter had to change his mind after years of following Jesus. Where might God be asking you to give up a partiality?
Do you know the date of your Baptism? How could your family mark that day each year?

lead: Ordinary Time begins, and on its first weekday two beginnings are read. The Letter to the Hebrews opens with God speaking at last “by a Son”, and in Mark that Son begins to speak: “The time is fulfilled.” The psalm sings of the Lord as King, and the same Son who is above the angels walks along a lakeshore and calls fishermen. God's final word has an address, and it asks for an answer.

r.h: God has spoken by a Son
set: In the first weeks of Ordinary Time, in this Year I, the Church reads Hebrews on weekdays. Hebrews calls itself “a word of exhortation” (13:22): it is a sermon, probably for Christians of Jewish background who were growing tired. Its author is not named; the Church received it among the letters linked with St Paul. It opens with some of the finest Greek in the New Testament: vv. 1–4 are a single long sentence.
str: vv. 1–2a: God spoke then through the prophets, now by a Son.
vv. 2b–4: who the Son is: heir, creator, reflection of the Father, purifier from sin, seated at God's right.
vv. 5–6: Scripture shows that he is greater than the angels.
kw: Two long words beginning with the same sound. God's word in the past came in parts, through many voices. In the Son it comes whole.
The brightness that comes from a light. It cannot be separated from its source. The Book of Wisdom uses this word of Wisdom (Wisdom 7:26).
The mark a seal leaves in wax or a die on a coin. The word hypostasis beside it means God's very being. The Son shows exactly what the Father is.
vv: but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son,
The prophets are not set aside: it is the same God speaking. But what comes now is not one more message; the messenger is the message.
He is the reflection of God’s glory and the exact imprint of God’s very being,
Early Christians used words like these to speak of who Christ is. They stand behind the Creed's “Light from Light”.
“Let all God’s angels worship him.”
The quotation is from the Greek form of Deuteronomy 32:43. Verse 5 has already joined Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14. Hebrews thinks in Israel's Scriptures, and reads them as speaking of the Son.
ch: The Catechism quotes these opening lines to teach that there will be no other Word than this one (CCC 65), and it cites St John of the Cross: in giving us his Son, God has said everything to us at once, and he has no more to say (in substance). The Second Vatican Council begins its account of revelation in Christ with the same verses (Dei Verbum 4). Verse 6 is cited for the adoration of the angels around the Incarnate Word (CCC 333), and verse 3 for the Son's relationship with the Father (CCC 241).

set: The Baptism of the Lord was read yesterday, from the same chapter. Now John is arrested, and Mark at once shows Jesus in Galilee, the region ruled by Herod Antipas, who has put John in prison (6:17). The Sea of Galilee was a working place, with fishing towns along its shore. Rabbis' disciples usually chose their teachers. Here the teacher goes out and chooses.
str: vv. 14–15: the first words of Jesus in Mark: the whole message in a sentence.
vv. 16–18: Simon and Andrew are called.
vv. 19–20: James and John are called.
kw: Not the time on a clock, but the decisive moment. It “is fulfilled”: what the prophets waited for has arrived.
Literally “change your mind”. It is a change of the whole direction of life, not just regret. Mark's order is important: God has already come near, and that is why people can turn.
The word translated “arrested” in v. 14. Mark uses the same word for the handing over of Jesus (9:31; 14:41). The forerunner's road is already the road of the Lord.
vv: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news.”
Two facts and two commands. First comes what God has done, then what we must do.
And Jesus said to them, “Follow me and I will make you fish for people.”

Literally “come after me”. Jeremiah 16:16 used fishing for God's judgment. Here the image is turned around: they will go out to gather people into the kingdom. They use the trade they know, but Jesus makes something new of it: “I will make you”.
Immediately he called them; and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, and followed him.
“Immediately” is Mark's favourite word. The “hired men” show that this family had a small business. What they left was real, and Zebedee is not abandoned: he is left with workers.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the Kingdom with Mark 1:14–15 (CCC 541), and calls this call to conversion an essential part of the proclamation of the Kingdom (CCC 1427). It adds that conversion goes on throughout the Christian life, as an uninterrupted task for the whole Church (CCC 1428). The call of the fishermen stands at the head of all Christian vocation: each person called is called to him before being called to any work.

qa: Does “repent” just mean feeling sorry for my sins?

Sorrow is part of it, but the word is larger. The Catechism describes interior repentance as a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God with all our heart (CCC 1431). The fishermen leave their nets. Conversion shows up in what one does next.
study: Hebrews says God has spoken “by a Son”. How much time do you actually give to listening to him in the Gospels?
What nets, good and useful things, might the Lord be asking you to hold more loosely?

lead: Yesterday Hebrews placed the Son high above the angels. Today it brings him down, for a little while, lower than they are, and calls that his glory. The psalm asks, “what are human beings that you are mindful of them?”, and Hebrews answers by pointing to Jesus. In Mark the same authority enters a synagogue in Capernaum, and a spirit that knows him is told to be silent. He who is above everything has come to where we are.

set: Having shown the greatness of the Son, Hebrews now meets the hardest question: how can one so great have died? Its answer is Psalm 8. The psalm sings of the human race, little yet crowned, and of all things put under its feet. But, says the author, we do not yet see this. We see Jesus, the one in whom the human vocation has come true. The quotation follows the Greek Old Testament. Psalm 8:5 in Hebrew has “a little lower than God”; the Greek has “angels”.
str: vv. 5–8a: Psalm 8: God's plan for humanity.
vv. 8b–9: we do not yet see it, but we see Jesus.
v. 10: it was fitting that the pioneer should be made perfect through sufferings.
vv. 11–12: he is not ashamed to call us his brothers and sisters.
kw: The Greek can mean “a little” in degree or “a little” in time. Hebrews seems to play on the second: the humbling of the Son has an end.
One who goes first and opens a way, and also a founder or leader. The same word returns in 12:2. He goes ahead on the road on which we must follow.

To bring to the goal. It does not mean that Jesus was morally lacking. In the Greek Old Testament this verb is used in the consecration of priests (Exodus 29:9), and Hebrews will soon call him high priest.
vv: but we do see Jesus, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.
This is the first time the letter uses the human name “Jesus”, and the author puts it in a strong position. Glory comes through the suffering, not around it. “For everyone” leaves no one out.
It was fitting that God, for whom and through whom all things exist, in bringing many children to glory, should make the pioneer of their salvation perfect through sufferings.
“Fitting”: it was right that the God who wishes to bring his children home should send one who walks the whole road with them.
For this reason Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters,
Then v. 12 puts Psalm 22:22 on his lips. Psalm 22 is the psalm of the Cross, and its opening words are the cry of Jesus (Mark 15:34). Here its song of praise in the assembly becomes his too.
ch: “To the benefit of every man, Jesus Christ tasted death”, says the Catechism, citing this verse (CCC 629). Since Christ is the brother of each one, no human suffering is outside his family. Every Mass gathers those whom he calls brothers and sisters, “in the midst of the congregation”, to join him in praising the Father.

set: The Gospel continues directly from yesterday's call of the disciples. Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake and became the centre of the ministry in Galilee. The synagogue was the place where the local Jewish community gathered for Scripture and prayer, and Jesus, a faithful Jew, goes there on the sabbath. Scribes were the respected teachers of the Law, who taught by carefully handing on what they had received. Mark does not make fun of them. He is pointing to a difference that people noticed. This is the first miracle in Mark, and it is a victory over evil.
str: vv. 21–22: his teaching amazes them.
vv. 23–26: the man with the unclean spirit; the rebuke; the spirit goes out.
vv. 27–28: the people are amazed at a new teaching with authority; his fame spreads.
kw: Power that is one's own by right. Jesus does not lean on what others have said; he speaks from himself. His word does what it says, as the next scene shows.
A true title spoken by the wrong mouth. Compare James 2:19: the demons also believe, and shudder. To know who Jesus is, is not yet to love him.
“Be silent” in v. 25 is this strong verb, literally “be muzzled”. Mark uses it again when Jesus calms the storm (4:39). Whether in the sea or in the human heart, one word from him is enough.
vv: They were astounded at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Mark does not say here what he taught. The first thing he wants us to see is who is teaching.
“What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.”
The Holy One and the unclean spirit cannot live in the same place. The first in Mark to call him this is an enemy, who fears him.
He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.
Just before this they call it a new teaching with authority. The people link the teaching and the deed. For Mark they are one thing: Jesus' word is what sets the man at liberty.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 22 to say that Jesus was not content to offer his interpretation alongside others, but taught as one with authority (CCC 581). It teaches too that the coming of God's kingdom means the defeat of Satan's (CCC 550), and that the Church has received from Jesus the power and office of exorcizing (CCC 1673). That power is exercised in the Church's name and under the bishop's authority, and it should be distinguished from illness, which belongs to medical care (CCC 1673).

qa: How can Jesus, who is God, be made “perfect through sufferings”?

He was never morally imperfect: Hebrews says he was without sin (4:15). “Perfect” here means complete, brought to the goal. In his humanity he went through obedience and death, and so he became fully what he came to be: the priest and leader of his brothers and sisters. “Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (5:8).
study: Hebrews says Jesus is not ashamed to call you his brother or sister. What might you be ashamed of that he is not?
The spirit knew who Jesus was and hated him. How can your knowledge of the faith become love?

lead: Hebrews says today why the Son had to become like us in every respect: so that he might be merciful, and able to help. Mark shows that mercy at work on a single day in Capernaum: a sick woman lifted by the hand, a town at the door at sunset, and a man at prayer before dawn. The psalm calls us to “seek the Lord and his strength”. Both readings speak of one who comes very close, and who does not stay in any one place.

r.h: Like his brothers and sisters in every respect
set: The argument of yesterday's reading continues, the Lectionary leaping only v. 13. If the Son calls us brothers and sisters, he has to share what is ours. Here for the first time in the letter Jesus is called high priest (v. 17), the great theme that will fill chapters 4–10. Verse 16 names the people he came to help: not angels but “the descendants of Abraham”.
str: vv. 14–15: he shares flesh and blood in order to destroy death's power.
v. 16: he came to help the descendants of Abraham.
vv. 17–18: he had to be like us, to be a merciful and faithful high priest and to help those being tested.
kw: The one who represented the people before God, above all on the Day of Atonement. Hebrews alone in the New Testament gives this title to Jesus by name.
The two sides of a true priest: merciful towards the people, faithful towards God. These words sum up the rest of the letter.
The same word serves for both. He knows from within what it is to be tried. Hebrews adds later that he was “without sin” (4:15).
vv: Since, therefore, the children share flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared the same things,
This is the Incarnation in its simplest form. St Gregory of Nazianzus gave the reason in a famous line: what has not been assumed has not been healed.
Therefore he had to become like his brothers and sisters in every respect,
“Had to”, not because anything could force God, but because this is what mercy required. There is no part of our life that he has not touched from within, except sin.
Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested.
A word for anyone who feels that God cannot understand them. The Lord does not help us from a distance. He has been there.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 14–15 when it teaches that Christ, by dying, destroyed him who has the power of death and delivered those who were subject to lifelong bondage through fear of it (CCC 635). The Church's prayer at funerals rests on this hope. The fear of death has not vanished, but it no longer has the last word.

set: The Gospel continues directly from yesterday's scene in the synagogue, and it is still the same sabbath. Archaeologists at Capernaum have uncovered a house that early Christians honoured as a place of worship, and many think that it was Peter's. The people wait until sunset, probably because the sabbath ended then, and they could carry the sick. The story of this one full day ends in a very different place: in the dark, alone, in prayer.
str: vv. 29–31: Simon's mother-in-law is healed.
vv. 32–34: at sunset the whole town comes.
vv. 35–39: prayer before dawn, and the decision to move on.
kw: Mark says he “lifted her up” with the verb he will use for the Resurrection (16:6). A hand reaching out to a sick woman already shows what the Lord will do for all.

“She began to serve them.” It is the word for what Jesus says he came to do: “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). She is the first human being in Mark to do it (angels do it in 1:13), and the healed life at once becomes a life of service.
The same word as the wilderness in which John preached and Jesus was tempted (1:4, 12). Jesus goes back to the place of testing to be with his Father.
vv: He came and took her by the hand and lifted her up. Then the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
There is no word of power here, only a hand. The disciples told him about her (v. 30), and this is the simplest form of intercession: they told him.
In the morning, while it was still very dark, he got up and went out to a deserted place, and there he prayed.
After the busiest day so far, he gets up in the dark. Prayer was not what Jesus did when the work was done; it was where the work came from.
“Let us go on to the neighboring towns, so that I may proclaim the message there also; for that is what I came out to do.”
“Everyone is searching for you” (v. 37) is what success sounds like. He hears his mission in prayer, not in the crowd's applause, and it takes him further on.
ch: Christ's healings, the Catechism says, are a resplendent sign that “God has visited his people” (CCC 1503). Jesus often draws apart to pray in solitude, on a mountain, preferably at night (CCC 2602). The Church keeps that order in her own life: the morning prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours comes before the day's work.

qa: Was St Peter married?

Yes. A mother-in-law means a wife, and St Paul also mentions that Cephas took a believing wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). In the Latin Church today priests are normally chosen from men who live celibacy for the Kingdom, as a discipline and a gift; in the Eastern Churches married men may be ordained priests (CCC 1579–1580). Celibacy is not a judgment on marriage; both are ways of following the Lord.
rite: St Hilary of Poitiers, bishop and doctor, may be remembered today. In the fourth century he was sent into exile by the emperor for defending the faith of Nicaea, and he wrote his great work On the Trinity. Today's reading fits him well: he defended both the true divinity of the Son and the truth of his becoming our brother.
study: Whom could you “tell Jesus about” today, as the disciples told him about Simon's mother-in-law?
What is the first thing you do when you get up? How might you make room for even a short time of prayer before the day begins?

lead: “Today” is the word of the first reading. Hebrews takes Psalm 95, today's responsorial psalm, and says that God's call is always spoken now, and that a heart can grow hard by waiting. The Gospel shows a man who does not wait. He kneels, he asks, and he is touched, and in the end Jesus is the one who has to stay out in the country. Compassion takes the outsider's place.

r.h: Today, if you hear his voice
set: The Lectionary passes over 3:1–6, which compare Jesus with Moses. Now the author turns to warning, using a psalm that was part of Israel's own worship. Psalm 95 recalls the desert: at Massah and Meribah the people put God to the test (Exodus 17:1–7), and later they refused to enter the land (Numbers 14). The author is not speaking against the Jewish people. He writes to Christians, and he uses Israel's Scripture as a mirror for them. Hebrews 4 goes on with the theme of rest, as the reading of tomorrow will show.
str: vv. 7–11: Psalm 95: do not harden your hearts.
v. 12: take care: the danger of turning away from the living God.
v. 13: the remedy: exhort one another every day.
v. 14: what is at stake: being partners of Christ.
kw: The key word. The psalm was already an old one, and the author says that its “today” is still open. God's word is always addressed to the present.
A hard heart does not usually come from one great refusal, but from many small delays. Verse 13 speaks of “the deceitfulness of sin”.
Those who share. The word was used for partners in a shared work, as of the fishermen in Luke 5:7. We are not only helped by Christ; we are made sharers with him.
vv: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion,
The Holy Spirit is named as the speaker: Scripture is a word spoken now, not only one written long ago.
But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,”
No one should try to keep faith alone. The remedy against a hardening heart is another Christian who cares, and who speaks up every day.
For we have become partners of Christ, if only we hold our first confidence firm to the end.
A sermon for the tired. The first enthusiasm may fade, but the confidence it gave can be held on to. The race is not won at the start.
ch: The Catechism says that a word marks the Church's prayer: “Today!”, echoing the call of the Holy Spirit in Hebrews and Psalm 95 (CCC 1165). In the Liturgy of the Hours, Psalm 95 is the usual invitatory, the first psalm of the Church's day. So each morning priests, religious and many lay people begin with this warning and this invitation.

set: The tour of Galilee (1:39) continues. On the Law regarding skin disease, see Leviticus 13–14: the sick person lived alone, outside the camp, and had to warn others away (13:45–46). To be restored he had to be examined by a priest. The man in this story comes far closer than the rule expected, and Jesus goes further still by touching him. Matthew and Luke tell the story too; Mark's telling is the most vivid of the three.
str: v. 40: the man's request.
vv. 41–42: compassion, touch, word, healing.
vv. 43–44: the stern order: say nothing; go to the priest.
v. 45: the man proclaims it, and Jesus has to stay outside.
kw: From splanchna, the inner parts of the body. It is a gut feeling of compassion. The Gospels use this verb almost only of Jesus and of the figures in his parables who stand for God's mercy.

A very strong word that can suggest snorting with indignation. It is puzzling here. Jesus' feeling is not gentle only; perhaps he is confronting evil, and he does not wish to be known only as a wonder-worker.
This is the verb used for Jesus' own preaching (1:14, 38–39). Mark uses it for the healed man in v. 45. He disobeys the order, but he becomes, in spite of it, the first to spread the news.
vv: “If you choose, you can make me clean.”
He does not doubt the power; he only wonders about the will. Years of living apart had taught him not to expect to be wanted.
Moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, and said to him, “I do choose. Be made clean!”

A note on the text. Most manuscripts have “moved with pity” (splanchnistheis), as the NRSV and POC do. A few, chiefly Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses, have “moved with anger” (orgistheis). Some scholars favour this reading, as it is the harder one, and it would fit the strong verb of v. 43: anger at the disease and the isolation, not at the man. Either way, what Jesus does is the same: he touches him.
so that Jesus could no longer go into a town openly, but stayed out in the country;

The story ends with an exchange of places. The man who lived outside the towns now goes back among people, and Jesus is now the one outside. It already points to the Cross, “outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
ch: The Catechism says that moved by so much suffering, Christ not only allows himself to be touched by the sick, but makes their miseries his own (CCC 1505). Many saints have learned this at the feet of those with leprosy. St Francis of Assisi recalls in his Testament that the Lord led him among lepers, and what had seemed bitter became sweet. St Damien de Veuster went to live among the leprosy patients of Molokai in 1873 and died of the disease in 1889.

qa: When Hebrews says “they will not enter my rest”, does it mean that God has rejected the Jewish people?

No. Hebrews is warning its Christian hearers, with the same words Israel used in its own worship. The psalm warned one generation in the desert; it did not pass judgment on a people. The Church teaches that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839), and that the Jewish people must not be presented as rejected by God (Nostra Aetate 4).
rite: In India many remember today St Devasahayam, a court official in eighteenth-century Travancore who became a Christian and refused to treat people differently because of their caste. He was put to death on 14 January 1752 and was canonized by Pope Francis on 15 May 2022. Check the diocesan calendar. Like Jesus in today's Gospel, he reached across a barrier and bore the cost. We pray for those who suffer for their faith in many lands, and for those who wrong them.
study: Is there a call of God to which you have been answering “not today”? What would it mean to answer it now?
Who would be helped by a word of encouragement from you today? Whom would you most dread touching, and why?

lead: Both readings today are about getting in. Hebrews warns that a promise can stand wide open and still be missed, as it was missed by the generation in the desert. Mark tells of four men who find the door blocked by a crowd and go through the roof. Those who hardened their hearts stayed out; those who would not give up came in, and the man they carried received more than they asked. The key words are rest, faith and authority.

r.h: The rest that is still open
set: Hebrews is a sermon written to Christians who were growing tired. Its author is not named. Just before our reading (3:7–19) the preacher has quoted Psalm 95, “Today, if you hear his voice”, and recalled the generation of the Exodus, who refused to go into the land after the report of the spies (Numbers 14) and died in the desert. God’s word to them was, “They shall not enter my rest.”

Now the preacher makes a surprising move. He joins Psalm 95 to Genesis 2:2, where God rests on the seventh day. The rest that Israel missed was never only a piece of land. It is God’s own rest, open since creation and still offered.
str: vv. 1–2: the promise stands, so take care. Good news was heard then and is heard now.
vv. 3–5: believers enter. Two texts explain the rest: Psalm 95:11 and Genesis 2:2.
v. 11: the conclusion: make every effort.
¶ The Lectionary passes over vv. 6–10, where the preacher argues that Joshua did not give the final rest (v. 8), and so “a sabbath rest still remains for the people of God” (v. 9).
kw: The word of the Greek Psalm 95:11. A related verb stands in Genesis 2:2 for God’s rest. It does not mean idleness. It means sharing the peace of God, whose work is complete.
Not in today’s verses, but it is their goal. No earlier use of this word is known. The weekly sabbath becomes a sign of what is waiting at the end.
To hurry, to be in earnest. It is a striking word to set beside “rest”: this rest is worth working for.
vv: the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ here. Many of the oldest have a plural, as the NRSV translates: the people were not joined in faith with those who listened. Others have a singular: the message was not joined with faith in those who heard it. The Malayalam POC says more simply that they did not believe. The sense is the same: hearing alone did not save them.
For we who have believed enter that rest
The verb is in the present tense. The rest lies ahead, and yet believers are already on their way into it.
Let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall through such disobedience as theirs.
The preacher says “let us” and includes himself. Nobody in the Church is past the need for this warning.
ch: St Augustine opens his Confessions with the prayer that our heart is restless until it rests in God, and he closes The City of God with a picture of the seventh day without evening: “There we shall rest and see, we shall see and love, we shall love and praise”, as the Catechism quotes him (CCC 1720). The Sunday rest of Christians is a small weekly taste of that goal (CCC 2175, 2184–2185).

set: This passage opens a group of five controversy stories (Mark 2:1–3:6). The Lectionary reads all five on the weekdays from today to next Wednesday. Each one raises a question about who Jesus is, and the tension rises until the plot of 3:6.

Jesus has come back to Capernaum, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. “At home” probably means the house of Simon and Andrew (1:29). A house of that region had a flat roof of beams covered with branches and packed earth, reached by an outside stair. Digging through such a roof was possible, and repairing it was too.
str: vv. 1–2: the crowded house; Jesus is speaking the word.
vv. 3–4: four men, a mat, a hole in the roof.
v. 5: Jesus sees their faith and forgives.
vv. 6–10a: the silent objection and Jesus’ question.
vv. 10b–12: the healing, the amazement, the praise of God.
kw: A passive verb with no named doer. In Jewish speech of the time this was a reverent way of saying that God does the act. The scribes hear rightly that Jesus is speaking in God’s place.
Mark has already used it of Jesus’ teaching (1:22, 27). Now it reaches the place only God can reach.
This is the first time the title appears in Mark. It is Jesus’ own way of speaking of himself, and it recalls the one in Daniel 7:13–14 to whom God gives dominion.
vv: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”

Mark says “their” faith. The friends’ faith is seen in what they did. Everyone had come for a healing, and Jesus begins somewhere else. This does not mean that every illness is caused by the sick person’s sin. It means that the deepest need is met first.
Why does this fellow speak in this way? It is blasphemy! Who can forgive sins but God alone?
On this point the scribes are correct. Their reasoning is sound and they defend God’s honour. The only question left is who this man is.
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins

Forgiveness cannot be seen, and a walking man can. Jesus offers the visible act as a sign of the invisible one. “On earth” is the surprise: God’s pardon is now available here, through a man in a house in Capernaum.
ch: “Only God forgives sins”, the Catechism says, and since Jesus is the Son of God he says of himself that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (CCC 1441). This is why his words could scandalize sincere people (CCC 589). The Catechism places this very healing at the head of the sacraments of healing: the Lord who forgave and restored the paralytic wants his Church to continue this work (CCC 1421). Every absolution in the sacrament of Penance is the same authority at work.

qa: Does this story mean that the man’s illness was a punishment for his sin?

The text does not say so, and Jesus rejects that kind of reasoning elsewhere (John 9:1–3; Luke 13:1–5). Illness can be a heavy trial without being a punishment. Here Jesus shows that he has come to heal the whole person, soul and body.
study: Who has carried me to Jesus by their faith, and whom am I carrying now?
Hebrews says a promise can be heard and still not help us. What is the “today” in which God is asking me not to harden my heart?

lead: Hebrews today shows us two things about God’s nearness. His word is sharp enough to lay the heart bare, and our high priest is gentle enough to understand what he finds there. Mark shows the same pair in action: Jesus looks at a tax collector at his booth, sees everything, and says, “Follow me.” He then sits down at table with people others avoided. The word that exposes us is spoken by the one who calls us. The key words are word, mercy and call.

set: The preacher has just urged his hearers not to harden their hearts when they hear God’s voice “today”. Verses 12–13 explain why this matters: God’s word is not a dead record of what happened in the desert. It speaks now, and nothing can hide from it. Then at v. 14 the letter turns to its great theme, the priesthood of Christ, which will fill the chapters ahead.
str: vv. 12–13: God’s word is alive, and everything is open before him.
vv. 14–15: we have a high priest who has passed through the heavens and who understands.
v. 16: so let us approach.
kw: Literally “two-mouthed”, a sword sharp on both sides. The soul and spirit, joints and marrow of v. 12 are not a lesson in anatomy. Together they say that the word reaches the very depths of a person.
A rare verb, related to the word for neck, trachēlos. Scholars are not sure of the picture behind it. The sense is clear from “naked” beside it: nothing is covered.
Originally the right of a citizen to speak openly. In prayer it means simple confidence before God, the confidence of children (compare CCC 2778). The POC translates it “with hope”.
vv: Indeed, the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword

The Second Vatican Council cites this verse in its teaching on Scripture in the life of the Church: the word of God is the strength of the Church’s faith and food for the soul (Dei Verbum 21). When we read Scripture, it also reads us.
For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin.

Two negatives make the point gently: it is not that he cannot understand. “Without sin” does not make him less able to sympathize. Someone who never gives in to a temptation feels its full force. The Council of Chalcedon drew on this verse: like us in all things but sin (CCC 467).
Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

Many commentators hear in “throne of grace” an echo of the mercy seat over the ark, where the high priest brought the blood once a year. What only one man could approach, on one day, all the faithful are now told to approach, in every time of need.
ch: The Catechism applies v. 15 to the temptations of Jesus in the desert: he conquered the tempter for us (CCC 540). It also quotes the Council on the power of Scripture: the force and power in the word of God is so great that it stands as the support and energy of the Church (CCC 131; Dei Verbum 21). Before the “throne of grace” the Church brings every kind of need at the Mass, in the Prayer of the Faithful.

r.h: The call at the tax booth
set: Capernaum lay near the border between the territories of Herod Antipas and his brother Philip, on a trade road, and so a toll post there makes good sense. A toll collector such as Levi worked for those who held the contract, under the authority of Herod. Collectors were known for overcharging, and they dealt constantly with Gentiles and with their money. Many devout people therefore kept apart from them.
Mark calls this man Levi son of Alphaeus. Matthew’s Gospel tells the same story of a man named Matthew (Matthew 9:9), and the Church has traditionally understood them to be one person.
str: vv. 13–14: Jesus teaches by the sea, then calls Levi.
v. 15: a meal with many tax collectors and sinners.
v. 16: the question put to the disciples.
v. 17: Jesus answers with a proverb and a statement of his mission.
kw: A man who collected tolls and duties, rather than a high official. Neither wealth nor position would make him welcome among the devout.

The word for discipleship in Mark. Levi’s rising and following repeats the call of the first four (1:16–20). In his case there is more to leave behind: a fisherman can go back to the boat, but a toll collector would not easily get his post back.
The same verb is used for inviting guests to a meal. In v. 17 both senses work: Jesus calls sinners to follow him, and he invites them to his table.
vv: As he was walking along, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.”

There is no test, no promise from Levi, no mention of repentance beforehand. The gaze and the word come first, and the change follows. St Bede says in a homily that Jesus saw the tax collector with a look of mercy and of choosing, miserando atque eligendo. Pope Francis took those words as his motto (Misericordiae Vultus 8).
“Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

In that culture to share a table meant to share life and to accept one another. The Pharisees’ question came from a real concern for holiness. They wanted all of life to be lived in purity before God. The question is what holiness does when it meets a sinner.
Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I have come to call not the righteous but sinners.

This is a proverb, and then a statement of why he has come. There is some irony in the word “righteous”. Jesus is not saying that some people have no need of him. He is saying that nobody can receive a physician without admitting to being ill.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom (CCC 545), and that receiving them at his table expresses in an astonishing way both God’s forgiveness and their return to the People of God (CCC 1443). It also notes that this conduct scandalized some Pharisees (CCC 588). Before Communion the Church invites us to the supper of the Lamb, and we answer that we are not worthy.

qa: Does Jesus’ eating with sinners mean that sin does not matter?

No. He calls sinners the sick, and a physician does not treat illness as if it were nothing. Levi gets up and follows, and his life changes. Mercy comes first, and it leads to conversion (compare Mark 1:15; CCC 1427–1428).
study: When I read Scripture, do I let it read me? Which verse has laid something bare in me?
Who today is treated as Levi was, and how would Jesus look at that person? How would I?

lead: Christmas is over and the Baptism of the Lord has closed the season. On this first Sunday of green vestments the Church asks a plain question: how does a person come to know God? All the readings answer it in terms of hearing, following and belonging. A boy in the sanctuary at Shiloh keeps running to the wrong person until an old priest teaches him to say, “Speak, for your servant is listening.” The psalm answers with the same readiness: “Here I am.” Two disciples at the Jordan hear John’s word about the Lamb of God, follow Jesus, and are asked what they are looking for.

Between them St Paul reminds the Corinthians that this call claims the whole person: “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.” God’s call comes through other people, Eli for Samuel, John for the disciples, Andrew for his brother. And it does not stay in the mind. The key words are listen, come and see and body.

r.h: Speak, for your servant is listening
set: The First Book of Samuel tells how Israel passed from the time of the judges to the time of the kings. Samuel stands on the bridge between them. He is the son of Hannah, who prayed for a child in her barrenness and gave him back to the Lord (1 Samuel 1). He serves as a boy at the sanctuary of Shiloh, where the ark of the covenant was kept, under the old priest Eli.

The sanctuary is in a bad state. Eli’s sons abuse their office (2:12–17), and Eli does not restrain them (3:13). The chapter opens with a sad note: “The word of the Lord was rare in those days; visions were not widespread” (3:1). Into that silence, God speaks to a child.
str: v. 3b: night in the sanctuary: the lamp, the boy, the ark.
vv. 4–9: three calls. Samuel runs to Eli each time, until Eli understands and teaches him the answer.
v. 10: the Lord comes and stands there, and Samuel answers.
v. 19: Samuel grows up, and none of his words fall to the ground.

¶ The Lectionary passes over vv. 11–18, the hard message against Eli’s house, which Eli accepts when the boy tells it: “It is the Lord; let him do what seems good to him” (3:18). The words Samuel has learned to hear are not always easy words.
kw: Abraham’s answer (Genesis 22:1), Moses’ answer (Exodus 3:4), Isaiah’s answer (Isaiah 6:8). It says more than where a person is standing. It means “I am at your disposal.” Samuel says it four times in vv. 4–8, and three of those times he says it to the wrong person.
Not simply to have information. Samuel served the Lord every day and yet “did not yet know the Lord” (v. 7). To know God in the Bible is to be in a living relationship with him.
From šāma‘, to hear, the same verb Hebrew uses for obeying. To listen properly is already to be ready to do.
vv: the lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.
The lamp burned through the night (Exodus 27:20–21), so the hour is before dawn. The narrator may also mean more than the time: the old order is growing dark, but God’s light has not gone out.
Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.
This verse explains why he keeps going to Eli. It also comforts us. A person can be faithful, and close to holy things, and still be waiting for the moment when it becomes personal.
Then Eli perceived that the Lord was calling the boy.

Eli has failed as a father and as a priest, and his eyes are dim. Yet he has one thing left to give, and he gives it honestly: he points the boy away from himself toward God, even though he must suspect what God may say about his house. Often God’s call needs a human helper who can recognize it.
‘Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.’
This is the prayer Eli teaches. It is one of the best short prayers in the Bible, and it is a prayer of listening, not of asking.
Samuel said, “Speak, for your servant is listening.”
The boy leaves out the word “Lord”, both in the NRSV and in the POC. Perhaps he does not yet dare to say it. The text does not explain.
As Samuel grew up, the Lord was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.
Words that fall to the ground are words that come to nothing. The one who listened to God’s word now speaks a word that God keeps. The silence of v. 1 is broken.
ch: The Catechism uses this very scene in teaching about prayer: the child Samuel must have learned from his mother Hannah how to stand before the Lord, and from the priest Eli how to listen to his word, “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening” (CCC 2578). The Church also sees here how a vocation is usually discerned: a person hears something he cannot yet name, and someone wiser helps him to name it.

set: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus (16:8), probably about the middle of the fifties, to a young Church he had founded. Corinth was a busy port city and a Roman colony. Some of the believers there held that because they had received the Spirit, what they did with their bodies no longer mattered.

Just before our reading Paul quotes what many scholars think were their own slogans: “All things are lawful for me” and “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food” (6:12–13). The reasoning seems to have gone like this: as food is for the stomach, so sex is for the body, and both are passing away. Paul’s answer takes the body seriously because God does.
str: vv. 13c–14: the body is for the Lord. God raised the Lord and will raise us.
v. 15a: your bodies are members of Christ.
v. 17: united to the Lord, one spirit with him.
v. 18: flee from fornication.
vv. 19–20: a temple, bought with a price, so glorify God.
kw: For Paul this is not a shell that a person lives in. It is the whole person as present in the world, able to relate and to act. That is why the body can belong to the Lord, and why it will be raised.
A broad word for sexual relations outside marriage. Paul’s surrounding verses speak of prostitution, a well known feature of a port town, but the principle reaches further.
The word for the sanctuary itself, the place of God’s presence. Earlier Paul said that the community is God’s temple (3:16). Here he applies the same word to each believer’s body.

From agora, the marketplace. The price is not named, but the reader knows what it was: the Cross. A slave who is bought belongs to a new master. Here the new master is the Lord, and belonging to him is true liberty (compare 7:22–23).
vv: The body is meant not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
The second half is the surprise. It is easy to say that the body is for the Lord; Paul also says the Lord is for the body. Christ does not save only souls.
But anyone united to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
The verb means to be closely joined, the language of Genesis 2:24, which Paul has just quoted in v. 16. No union with Christ leaves the body outside it.
Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against the body itself.

This is a hard saying, since other sins too involve the body. Some scholars think the first half is another Corinthian slogan, and others think Paul is speaking loosely. His point is clear in either case: this sin touches the person in a singular way. The Church’s teaching on human love explains why: the body speaks the language of total self-giving, and here that language is used without the gift.
do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God, and that you are not your own?

The word “you” is plural and “body” is singular, as if each person’s body and all of them together were held in view. “You are not your own” is a hard sentence in any age, and it is good news: we belong to someone who paid dearly for us.
For you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.
Paul’s last word is positive. He gives no list of rules here. The body is an instrument of praise.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage in its teaching on the resurrection: the dignity of the body comes from the fact that it belongs to Christ and will share his risen life (CCC 1004). The human body shares in the dignity of the image of God, and the whole person is meant to become a temple of the Spirit (CCC 364). Baptism makes us temples of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). The Church’s teaching on chastity (CCC 2337) and on sexual relations outside marriage (CCC 2353) rests on this view of the person. St John Paul II returned to this passage in his catecheses on human love.

set: The Fourth Gospel opens with a sequence of days around the Jordan (1:29, 35, 43). John the Baptist has been asked who he is, and he has answered that he is not the Messiah. Now he does the last thing a witness can do: he points away from himself and lets his disciples go.

The Lectionary follows the Gospel of Mark this year, but on this Sunday it reads St John in all three years, because the Second Sunday continues the showing of the Lord that Epiphany celebrates (Introduction to the Lectionary, 105). St Mark’s Gospel takes up the Sunday course next week.
str: vv. 35–36: John points to Jesus: “Look, here is the Lamb of God!”
v. 37: two disciples follow.
vv. 38–39: Jesus’ first words, and the afternoon with him.
vv. 40–41: Andrew finds his brother.
v. 42: Jesus looks at Simon and gives him a new name.
kw: John has used this title already (1:29). It gathers up the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the servant led like a lamb (Isaiah 53:7). At the end of this Gospel, the words about the lamb’s bones are applied to Jesus on the Cross (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46).

It comes three times in vv. 38–39: where are you staying, where he was staying, they remained. The disciples are asking for an address, and John’s reader hears more, because the same verb returns in chapter 15: “Abide in me as I abide in you.”
The Greek spelling of the Hebrew and Aramaic word for “anointed one”. In the whole New Testament only John’s Gospel keeps this form (here and 4:25), and he explains it: Christos, Anointed.

From the Aramaic kêpā’, a rock. Petros is the Greek for it. Paul too often calls the apostle Cephas (1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9). When God gives a new name in the Bible, he gives a new mission, as with Abraham (Genesis 17:5) and Israel (Genesis 32:28).
vv: and as he watched Jesus walk by, he exclaimed, “Look, here is the Lamb of God!”

The verb for “watched” means to look intently, and it comes back in v. 42 when Jesus looks at Simon. John’s whole ministry ends in this pointing finger. Greatness in the Kingdom can be measured by how readily one lets others go to Jesus.
When Jesus turned and saw them following, he said to them, “What are you looking for?”

These are the first words of Jesus in the Fourth Gospel, and they are a question. He does not begin by telling them what they ought to want. He says something similar at the empty tomb to Mary Magdalene: “Whom are you looking for?” (20:15). The question is put to everyone who reads this Gospel.
He said to them, “Come and see.”
He gives no explanation, and offers no course of instruction. Discipleship in John begins by spending time with him. Philip will use the same words to invite Nathanael (1:46).
It was about four o’clock in the afternoon.

The Greek says “the tenth hour”, as the POC keeps it. Many readers hear in this small detail the memory of someone who was there and never forgot the hour his life changed. The second disciple is not named. An old tradition sees in him the Beloved Disciple, but the Gospel does not say so.
He first found his brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah”
Andrew says “we have found”, though in truth he was found. The one who has met Jesus goes first to his own family.
He brought Simon to Jesus, who looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John. You are to be called Cephas”

Andrew’s whole achievement is summed up in the word “brought”. Jesus says who Simon is and who he will become. The future tense is a promise, and it will take this man a long and painful time to grow into it.
ch: The Church’s reading of this passage is heard at every Mass. Just before Communion the priest holds up the Host and repeats John’s words, “Behold the Lamb of God”. The Catechism teaches that John points out in Jesus the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, and so shows that Jesus is both the Suffering Servant and the Paschal Lamb (CCC 608). It presents Simon, the one whom the Lord named Peter, as the rock of his Church (CCC 552, 881). And what Andrew does is what the Catechism says of the first disciples: they burned with the desire to proclaim Christ and to lead others to faith in him (CCC 425). St John Chrysostom says that Andrew, after staying with Jesus, did not keep the treasure to himself but hurried to his brother (in substance).

qa: Why did Samuel not recognize God’s voice, if he lived in the sanctuary?

The text tells us: he “did not yet know the Lord” (3:7), and visions were rare in those days (3:1). Serving in holy things and meeting God personally are not the same. This is why parents, priests and spiritual guides matter: Eli could not hear the voice himself, but he recognized what was happening.
Does Paul look down on the body?

The opposite. He opposes those who said that the body did not matter. For Paul the body belongs to the Lord, is a temple of the Spirit, and will be raised. Sexual sin is serious in his eyes because the body is so precious. And the same Paul who says “Shun fornication!” announces a Lord who bought us at great price, so a person who has fallen comes back to mercy, in the sacrament of Penance, and never to despair (CCC 1422, 1465).
In the other Gospels Jesus calls Peter and Andrew by the lake, and Peter is named later. Which is right?

The Gospels do not all tell the story in the same order. Mark 1:16–20 (next Sunday’s Gospel) tells of the call beside the Sea of Galilee, and Matthew 16:18 tells of the naming at Caesarea Philippi. Many readers think that John records an earlier first meeting at the Jordan, which would explain why the fishermen responded so readily by the lake. Each evangelist arranged his material for his own purpose, and the Church teaches that they handed on the truth about Jesus (Dei Verbum 19; CCC 126).
rite: This Sunday belongs to the first stretch of Ordinary Time, between Christmas and Lent, when the vestments are green and the Sunday Gospels begin to tell of the public life of Jesus. Tomorrow the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity begins in many countries (18 to 25 January), and Andrew leading his brother to Jesus is a good picture for that prayer: Christians draw closer to each other as they draw closer to him. Next Sunday is the Sunday of the Word of God, set by Pope Francis on the Third Sunday in Ordinary Time (Aperuit Illis, 2019). Samuel’s prayer is a good way to prepare for it.
study: Samuel needed Eli to help him recognize God’s voice. Who has done this for me? For whom might I do it?
Try Samuel’s prayer before reading Scripture this week: “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.” What is the difference between this prayer and the way I usually pray?
“You are not your own.” How does that sentence sound to me? What would it mean to glorify God in my body, in the way I eat, work, rest and love?
Jesus asks, “What are you looking for?” How would I answer him today? To whom could I say, “Come and see”?

lead: Hebrews today looks at Jesus in the days of his flesh, praying with loud cries and tears, and learning obedience through suffering. Mark shows him in the days of his flesh too, the bridegroom among his friends, and he says quietly that the day will come when he will be taken away. Joy and sorrow are not opposed here: the one who is the Church’s joy is the one who suffered for her. The key words are high priest, bridegroom and new.

set: The preacher has just invited his hearers to approach the throne of grace (4:16). Now he explains what kind of priest is waiting there. First he lists what a high priest needs, as seen in the priesthood of Aaron, then he shows how Christ meets those needs in a greater way. Two texts carry the argument, Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 110:4, the psalm the Lectionary gives us today.
Melchizedek, named here for the first time in the letter, will be taken up at length in chapter 7.
str: vv. 1–4: the high priest: taken from among mortals, gentle because weak, and called by God.
vv. 5–6: Christ did not appoint himself: two psalms.
vv. 7–10: his prayer and his suffering: he is made perfect and becomes the source of salvation.
kw: A rare word for keeping one’s feelings in measure, neither harsh nor indulgent. The high priest shares human weakness and so can be patient with the weak.

A play on words in the Greek, and a saying known among the Greeks that one learns by suffering. As Son he always loved the Father. As man he came to know obedience from the inside, in the suffering it cost him.

This does not mean that Jesus had moral faults to overcome (4:15 excludes that). The verb means to bring to completion, and in the Greek Old Testament it is used for the consecration of priests (Exodus 29:9). Through his Passion and glory he is fully established in his office as Saviour.
vv: He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is subject to weakness

This applies to priests of the old order, and the preacher will note where Christ differs: he has no sins of his own to offer for (v. 3; 7:27). But every Catholic priest can take the verse to heart. He offers the sacrifice as a sinner among sinners.
In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.

Most readers think of Gethsemane and the Cross, though the text does not name them. It goes further than the Gospels: “loud cries and tears”. But how was he “heard”, since he did die? He was not spared death. He was brought through it, in the Resurrection.
Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered; and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him
Notice the word “obey” in both places. His obedience becomes the source of ours. The one who learned obedience now saves those who learn it from him.
ch: The Catechism sees all the troubles and petitions of humanity gathered up in the cry of the incarnate Word on the Cross, and sees the Father answer them, beyond all hope, by raising his Son (CCC 2606). It quotes v. 8 in explaining the prayer “Thy will be done”: how much more reason have we sinful creatures to learn obedience (CCC 2825). The Council of Trent’s teaching that Christ is the source of eternal salvation by his Passion is taken up in CCC 617. Every ministerial priesthood is understood by the Church only as a sharing in his one priesthood (CCC 1544–1545).

set: This is the third of the five controversy stories. Fasting was a serious part of Jewish piety. The Law commanded it on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31), and devout people added other days; Luke mentions a Pharisee who fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). Mark says that John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. The surprise is that those around Jesus, who is plainly a man of God, are not. The question is not hostile, and it is a fair one.
str: v. 18: the question about fasting.
vv. 19–20: the bridegroom: now no fast; one day there will be.
vv. 21–22: two short sayings: the patch and the wineskins.
kw: In the prophets, God himself is Israel’s husband (Hosea 2:16–20; Isaiah 54:5; 62:5). Jesus takes this image for himself, without explanation. It is a large claim made in a few words.
A strong verb for removing someone. This is the first shadow of the Passion in Mark’s Gospel, in a conversation about a wedding.
A leather bag for wine. New wine is still fermenting and stretching its container; an old skin has lost its give and bursts.
vv: The wedding guests cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, can they?

A wedding in that world could last for days and was the happiest occasion a village knew. Nobody fasts at the wedding. By this image Jesus says that the time of waiting has given way to the time of fulfilment.
The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast on that day.

Jesus does not abolish fasting. He places it after his Passion. The Church’s fasting looks to Christ’s absence and to his return. Some have seen in “that day” a reference to the Friday of his death. The Christian fast is not the fast of those who have no bridegroom. It is the fast of those who love him and long for him.
but one puts new wine into fresh wineskins.

The sayings warn against patching and pouring: what Jesus brings cannot simply be added to life as it was. They do not say that the old cloak and the old wine were bad. Elsewhere Jesus praises the scribe who brings out of his treasure “what is new and what is old” (Matthew 13:52), and says that he has not come to abolish the law (Matthew 5:17).
ch: The Catechism points out that the Lord referred to himself as the bridegroom in this very verse, and that the Church is the bride (CCC 796). The Church keeps the days of fasting and abstinence in this spirit: the Fridays of the year and the season of Lent are days of penance (CCC 1438; Code of Canon Law, cann. 1250–1251). The Church does not read “new wine” as contempt for Israel. Jesus himself came to fulfil the Law, not to abolish it (CCC 577–582).

qa: Why should Catholics fast at all, if the bridegroom has risen and is with us?

He is with us, and yet we still wait to see him. Both are true. That is why the Church does not fast on Sundays, the days of the Resurrection, but does fast at other times. Fasting opens the heart for prayer and for the poor, and it joins us to the Lord in his Passion (CCC 540, 1434, 1438).
study: Hebrews says that Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears. Do I allow myself to pray like that? What would I bring?
What does fasting mean in my life? Does it bring me closer to the bridegroom and to the poor, or is it only a rule?

lead: Hope needs something to hold on to. Hebrews gives it two things: God’s promise and God’s oath, and pictures hope as an anchor thrown not down but up, through the curtain, where Jesus has already gone. In Mark the disciples pluck grain on the sabbath and Jesus answers with the deepest thing that can be said about that holy day: it is God’s gift, and he is its Lord. Both readings point to a God whose word and whose law are for our life. The key words are anchor, forerunner and sabbath.

set: The preacher has just written one of the sternest passages in the letter, about those who fall away (6:4–8). Now he changes his tone: “we are confident of better things in your case” (6:9). He remembers their love, then urges them on with the example of Abraham, who waited patiently, and with God’s own oath (Genesis 22:16–17). At the end he brings the argument back to Melchizedek, ready for chapter 7.
str: vv. 10–12: God remembers your love; keep going to the end.
vv. 13–15: the promise to Abraham, sworn by God himself.
vv. 16–18: why an oath: two unchangeable things.
vv. 19–20: hope, the anchor; Jesus, the forerunner.
kw: Used already at 5:11 for those who have grown dull in hearing. It is the real danger of this letter’s readers: tiredness rather than open rebellion.

Hope was pictured as an anchor among Greek writers too. Hebrews is the only place in the Bible where the word is used in this way. Christians later carved the anchor on tombs in the catacombs of Rome.
A runner sent ahead, a scout or advance party. It says that where Jesus has gone, others are to follow.
vv: For God is not unjust; he will not overlook your work and the love that you showed for his sake in serving the saints, as you still do.
The “saints” are simply the fellow believers. To tired people the preacher says first of all: God has seen it. No act of love is forgotten.
so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible that God would prove false, we who have taken refuge might be strongly encouraged to seize the hope set before us.
The two things are the promise and the oath. God does not need an oath to be truthful. He gives one for our sake, because we find it hard to trust. This is great courtesy on God’s part.
We have this hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters the inner shrine behind the curtain, where Jesus, a forerunner on our behalf, has entered

The image changes in the middle. An anchor goes down into the dark and holds the ship. This one goes up, behind the curtain of the Holy of Holies (Leviticus 16:2), where only the high priest went, once a year. Our hope is fastened where we cannot yet see, to someone who has already arrived.
ch: The Catechism quotes this very image in explaining the virtue of hope: hope is “the sure and steadfast anchor of the soul”, which enters where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf (CCC 1820). It also presents Abraham as the model of hope against hope (CCC 1819). Hope is more than a mood. It rests on what God has already done in Christ.

set: This is the fourth of the controversy stories, and the first to deal with the sabbath. The sabbath was and is a great gift of God to Israel, a sign of creation (Exodus 20:8–11) and of liberation from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:12–15). Picking some ears from a neighbour’s field with the hand was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25). The objection is about the day: the Law forbade harvest work on the sabbath (Exodus 34:21), and later Jewish tradition, in the Mishnah, lists reaping among thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work.
str: vv. 23–24: the disciples pluck grain, and the Pharisees object.
vv. 25–26: Jesus answers from Scripture: David and the bread of the Presence.
vv. 27–28: two sayings: the sabbath for humankind; the Son of Man is its Lord.
kw: The word of the objection in v. 24, and it returns in v. 26. The question is not a trivial one: for a devout Jew, keeping the sabbath was a way of loving God.
The twelve loaves set before the Lord in the sanctuary, renewed each sabbath and eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). So the argument from David also touches the sabbath.
The climax. Mark’s reader knows the word as a title of God and of the risen Jesus.
vv: Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the sabbath?

Jesus is held responsible for what his disciples do, which was normal for a teacher. He does not deny the Law, and he does not call the objection foolish. He argues from Scripture, as one Jewish teacher with others.
He entered the house of God, when Abiathar was high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence

The story is in 1 Samuel 21:1–6. Human need took precedence over a holy rule. The argument also has a hidden point: if David and his companions could do it, what about one greater than David and his companions?
The sabbath was made for humankind, and not humankind for the sabbath; so the Son of Man is lord even of the sabbath.

The first half is an insight some Jewish teachers also voiced. A later rabbinic saying, attributed to Rabbi Simeon ben Menasya, says that the sabbath is given to you, and not you to the sabbath (Mekhilta on Exodus 31:14). It is the second half that is new. Who can be lord of the day that God blessed?
ch: “Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of this day”, the Catechism teaches. He gives the sabbath law “its authentic and authoritative interpretation”, and this passage is quoted there (CCC 2173). Christians keep Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, which fulfils the spiritual truth of the sabbath (CCC 2175–2176). St John Paul II wrote at length on this link in Dies Domini (1998). So Sunday is not a burden but a gift: a day to worship God, to rest, and to do good to others (CCC 2184–2186).

qa: 1 Samuel 21 says that the priest was Ahimelech, not Abiathar. Is Mark mistaken?

This is a real difficulty. In 1 Samuel 21 the priest is Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father (1 Samuel 22:20). Matthew and Luke tell the story without giving the name. Some think that the phrase may mean “in the time of Abiathar” or “in the passage about Abiathar”, since Abiathar is the better known figure. Others think that a slip entered in the telling. The Church teaches that Scripture teaches without error “that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation” (Dei Verbum 11), and the point Jesus makes here is not affected by the name.
study: Hope is an anchor fastened where I cannot see. What is holding me steady now, and what in my life tests that hold?
What is my Sunday like? Is it a burden, a day like any other, or a gift from the Lord who made it for me?

lead: Today Hebrews reads a brief, strange story in Genesis and finds a portrait of Christ: a priest with no recorded beginning or end, who stands outside the line of Aaron. Mark brings the five controversy stories to their end in a synagogue. Jesus restores a withered hand, and the first plot against his life begins. The priest of “an indestructible life” is the one men already want to destroy. The key words are Melchizedek, indestructible and hardness of heart.

set: Melchizedek appears in only two places in the Old Testament. In Genesis 14:18–20 he comes out to meet Abraham, who is returning from battle, with bread and wine, blesses him and receives a tenth. In Psalm 110:4 the Lord swears to the king, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews puts these two texts together.

This matters to the preacher’s argument because Jesus was of the tribe of Judah, not of Levi (7:14), so he could not be a priest by descent. Psalm 110 shows that God had spoken of another kind of priesthood, older than Aaron’s.
str: vv. 1–2: the Genesis story and the meaning of the name.
v. 3: what Genesis does not say.
vv. 15–17: another priest arises: by power of life, not by descent.
kw: A Hebrew name meaning “my king is righteousness”, or as the letter puts it, “king of righteousness”. He is king of Salem, a name that sounds like šālôm, peace. Jewish tradition and Psalm 76:2 link Salem with Jerusalem.
Found only here in the New Testament. Priests in Israel had to prove their descent (Ezra 2:62). Genesis, which is so careful with family lists, names no father for this priest.
Something that cannot be taken apart or dissolved. The priesthood of Jesus does not rest on a family line that death keeps interrupting, but on his risen life.
vv: His name, in the first place, means “king of righteousness”; next he is also king of Salem, that is, “king of peace.”
Righteousness first, then peace. Readers of the letter will find both joined in Christ, who is our righteousness and our peace.
Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.

The preacher is not saying that Melchizedek literally had no parents or was an angel. He reads the silence of Genesis in the way that Jewish teachers of his time could read Scripture: what the text does not say can also teach. Note the direction: Melchizedek resembles the Son of God, and not the other way round. The Son is the original.
one who has become a priest, not through a legal requirement concerning physical descent, but through the power of an indestructible life.
Earlier priests died, and others took their place (7:23). This priest died, and lives. The Resurrection is what makes his priesthood last forever.
ch: “Christian tradition considers Melchizedek”, says the Catechism, “as a prefiguration of the priesthood of Christ” (CCC 1544), and it sees his offering of bread and wine as a figure of the Church’s own offering (CCC 1333). Hebrews itself does not mention the bread and wine, but the Fathers took this up, St Cyprian among them, in his letter on the Eucharistic cup (in substance). In the Roman Canon, Eucharistic Prayer I, the priest asks God to accept our gifts as he accepted “the offering of your high priest Melchizedek”. The priests of the Church share in this one priesthood of Christ (CCC 1545).

set: This is the last of the five controversy stories (2:1–3:6). It is also a sabbath story, and it follows at once on the grainfields. Those watching Jesus in the synagogue are not named until v. 6. Jewish teaching allowed for saving a life on the sabbath (later set down in Mishnah Yoma 8:6). A withered hand was not an emergency, and it could have waited one more day. This is the point at issue.
str: vv. 1–2: the man, the watchers, the sabbath.
vv. 3–4: Jesus calls the man to the centre and asks a question. They are silent.
v. 5: anger, grief, a word, the hand restored.
v. 6: the plot.
kw: To watch with hostile intent, as one might watch for a slip. Those watching have their eyes on the wrong thing: not the suffering man but the healer.
The word means a callus or something turning to stone. In Mark it is a warning for insiders, and later the disciples too are said to have hardened hearts (6:52; 8:17).
Supporters of the house of Herod. They were normally not allies of the Pharisees, which makes their agreement here striking. They appear again at Mark 12:13.
vv: Is it lawful to do good or to do harm on the sabbath, to save life or to kill?

Jesus moves the question from what work is allowed to what the day is for. Not to do good, when one could, is already to do harm. Meanwhile they are plotting on the sabbath to destroy a life, which is the irony Mark wants us to see.
He looked around at them with anger; he was grieved at their hardness of heart

Mark alone of the Gospels records the anger and the grief together. This is not the anger of a man who has been insulted. It is the anger of one who loves the man with the withered hand and those who are watching him. Matthew and Luke do not record the anger here.
The Pharisees went out and immediately conspired with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.

Jesus only spoke, and no labour was done. Still the conflict comes to a head. Mark speaks of a group of leaders in one town, not of the Jewish people. Many Pharisees were not hostile (see CCC 575, 595), and the Pharisees are not named among those who bring about Jesus’ death in Mark’s Passion.
ch: The Catechism draws on this verse in its teaching on the third commandment: “With compassion, Christ declares the sabbath for doing good rather than harm, for saving life rather than killing” (CCC 2173). It notes that from the beginning of his public ministry “certain Pharisees and partisans of Herod” agreed together to destroy him (CCC 574), and it firmly refuses to lay the blame for Jesus’ death on the Jews as a people (CCC 597–598). In the anger and the grief of Jesus the Church sees a true human heart: he “loved with a human heart” (Gaudium et Spes 22; CCC 470).

qa: Is it a sin to be angry, if Jesus was angry?

Anger as such is a passion, and the question is what it serves. The Catechism warns against anger that wants to harm (CCC 2302). The anger of Jesus here is joined to grief, it is aimed at a hardness that keeps people from mercy, and it ends in healing. That is the test of our anger.
rite: Today the Church may keep the optional memorials of St Fabian and St Sebastian. St Fabian was bishop of Rome and died a martyr in the persecution of Decius in 250. St Sebastian was a martyr of Rome, buried in the catacomb on the Appian Way that bears his name. The well known story of the arrows comes from a later account. Two witnesses gave their lives for the priest who lives forever.
study: Hebrews reads Scripture slowly enough to notice even its silences. What passage might I read more slowly this week?
The man was told to stretch out his withered hand. What part of my life has withered, and what would it mean to hold it out to Jesus?

lead: On the memorial of a young martyr, the weekday readings speak of two kinds of nearness to Jesus. Hebrews shows him seated at the right hand of God, always living to intercede for those who approach. Mark shows the crowds pressing on him from every region just to touch him, while the unclean spirits shout the right title for the wrong reason. To know who he is is not yet to belong to him. St Agnes, who gave him her whole life, shows what belonging means. The key words are intercede, once for all and Son of God.

r.h: He always lives to make intercession
set: The argument of chapter 7 reaches its end, and the preacher sums it up in 8:1: “the main point in what we are saying is this”. Levitical priests were many, because death kept removing them. They offered daily and offered for their own sins. Christ is one, lives forever, and offered once. Then the preacher takes up the next stage: if the priest is new, the sanctuary and the covenant must be new as well.
str: 7:25: he saves, because he lives and intercedes.
7:26–28: such a high priest: holy, once for all, a Son.
8:1–2: the main point: seated, a minister in the true tent.
8:3–5: the earthly sanctuary is a sketch and a shadow.
8:6: a better ministry and a better covenant.
kw: The Greek can mean either. The NRSV says “for all time”, and the POC says “completely”. Both are true of him: there is no limit to his saving power in time or in depth.
A key word in Hebrews (7:27; 9:12; 10:10). His sacrifice does not need repeating, for it is complete.
The word from which “liturgy” comes. Christ himself is the chief minister of the liturgy, in the heavenly sanctuary. Earthly liturgy is a sharing in that work.
vv: Consequently he is able for all time to save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
