This is one of the most comforting sentences in the New Testament. Jesus is not only the one who once died for me. He is the one who is praying for me now.
this he did once for all when he offered himself.
Here the priest and the victim are the same. No high priest of old could say that. Nothing remains to be added to what he offered.
They offer worship in a sanctuary that is a sketch and shadow of the heavenly one

The preacher quotes Exodus 25:40: Moses built according to the pattern shown on the mountain. A shadow is real, and it is cast by something. The old worship was God’s own gift and pointed beyond itself. The Church does not despise it and honours the covenant with Israel as never revoked (CCC 121, 839). The present tense has led many scholars to think the Temple was still standing when this was written, though others disagree.
he is the mediator of a better covenant, which has been enacted through better promises.

The preacher will now quote Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8:8–12). The Lord will say “this is my blood of the covenant” (Mark 14:24), which the Church hears at each Mass.
ch: The Catechism applies this verse to all of Christ’s life: he always lives to make intercession for us (CCC 519, 662), and in him all our intercession has its source (CCC 2634). It explains how the Mass and the ministerial priesthood stand to the “once for all”: the one sacrifice is made present and not repeated (CCC 1366–1367), and the one priesthood of Christ is made present through ministers, without diminishing its uniqueness. As St Thomas Aquinas says, “Only Christ is the true priest, the others being only his ministers” (CCC 1545).

set: After the plot of 3:6, Jesus withdraws to the lake, and Mark gives one of his summaries. The list of places covers almost the whole of the land of Israel and beyond: Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea in the south, the land east of the Jordan, and the coast of Tyre and Sidon in the north, which was Gentile territory. The word Idumea occurs only here in the New Testament. While the leaders plot, ordinary people are walking for days to reach him.
str: vv. 7–8: the great crowd and where it comes from.
vv. 9–10: the boat is kept ready, and the sick press forward.
vv. 11–12: the spirits cry out, and Jesus orders silence.
kw: Literally “a whip” or “scourge”, the word used here for illnesses. It tells how the sick felt their suffering.
The title of Mark’s first line (1:1). The heavenly voice has said it at the baptism (1:11). No human being says it in this Gospel until the centurion at the Cross (15:39).
The same verb that Jesus uses when he rebukes an unclean spirit (1:25) and the storm (4:39). He will not accept testimony from this source.
vv: for he had cured many, so that all who had diseases pressed upon him to touch him.
It is easy to see the crowd’s motives as mixed, and they surely were. Jesus does not send them away. Still, Mark shows him keeping a boat ready: even mercy needs some space to continue.
Whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and shouted, “You are the Son of God!” But he sternly ordered them not to make him known.

Their words are correct, but there is neither love nor obedience in them. Even the demons believe and shudder, as St James says (James 2:19). Why silence? The title cannot be rightly understood until the Cross and the Resurrection (9:9). Scholars call this theme in Mark “the Messianic secret”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ driving out of demons shows that the Kingdom of God has come, and anticipates his great victory over “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). It also says that the title “Son of God” is fully understood only through the Passion and Resurrection: in Mark it is the centurion before the Cross who says it (CCC 444). To know the right words is not enough. Faith is a personal adherence of the whole person to God (CCC 150, 176).

qa: If Christ’s sacrifice was once for all, what happens at Mass? Is he sacrificed again?

No. The Mass is not a new sacrifice added to the Cross. It is the one sacrifice of Christ made present, so that its saving power is applied to us today (CCC 1366–1367). Hebrews says that he lives forever and intercedes. His offering does not stop being present before the Father, and at the Mass the Church joins it.
rite: St Agnes is among the most loved martyrs of Rome, and she is named in the Roman Canon. She died probably at the beginning of the fourth century. St Ambrose wrote that she was only twelve years old (On Virgins, 1), and he marvels that a girl too small for the chains could face the sword without fear (in substance). Many details in later accounts are legendary, but her cult is very old, and a basilica stands over her tomb on the Via Nomentana. Her name recalls the Greek hagnē, pure, and to Latin ears agnus, lamb. So each year on this day two lambs are blessed in Rome, whose wool is woven into the pallium which the Pope gives to metropolitan archbishops. The readings suit her well: she went to the Lamb who always lives to intercede for us.
study: Jesus is praying for me now (Hebrews 7:25). How would it change my day if I really believed this?
The spirits knew his title but did not love him. Where in my faith do I have the right words but not yet the surrender?

lead: Both readings speak of a new beginning that grows out of Israel's own story. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's promise of a covenant written on the heart. Mark shows Jesus on a mountain, making twelve men the start of a renewed Israel. The psalm between them sings what such a covenant looks like: “Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet” (Psalm 85:10).

r.h: A covenant written on the heart
set: Since chapter 7 Hebrews has been arguing that Jesus is a high priest of a new kind. Chapter 8 turns from the priest to the covenant he serves. To make the point the author quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 in full, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament. Jeremiah's words belong to the time of the fall of Jerusalem (587 BC), when the people had lost nearly everything that seemed to hold the covenant up.
str: vv. 6–7: Jesus, mediator of a better covenant.
vv. 8–12: Jeremiah's oracle: not like the covenant of the Exodus, but written within.
v. 13: the author's conclusion about what is “new”.
kw: One who stands between two parties to bring them together. Hebrews uses this word of Jesus again at 9:15 and 12:24.
The Greek Old Testament's word for the Hebrew bĕrît. In ordinary Greek it also meant a will or testament, and Hebrews plays on that meaning at 9:16–17.
From palaios, old. The author draws this word out of Jeremiah's own word “new”, and he is speaking within his argument about the priesthood and the sanctuary.
vv: I will put my laws in their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
The law does not disappear. It changes place, from tablets of stone to the human heart. The last line is the oldest covenant promise of all, now kept from within.
For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.

Forgiveness is the foundation on which all of this stands. That is why Hebrews goes on at once to speak of Christ's blood. A note on the text: v. 9 follows the Greek Old Testament (“I had no concern for them”), while the Hebrew of Jeremiah 31:32 reads “though I was their husband”.
In speaking of “a new covenant,” he has made the first one obsolete.
Read this sentence with care. See the question below.
ch: The Catechism quotes these very words when it describes the New Law as the interior law of charity (CCC 1965), and adds St Thomas Aquinas's definition: the New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ (CCC 1966). St Augustine builds much of his work On the Spirit and the Letter on this oracle of Jeremiah: what the law commanded from outside, the Spirit gives from within (in substance). At every Mass the priest speaks of “the new and eternal covenant” over the chalice.

r.h: Twelve, to be with him and to be sent
set: Mark has been showing growing crowds and growing opposition from some leaders (3:6–12). Now Jesus leaves the crowd and goes up the mountain. In the Bible a mountain is a place of meeting with God, and readers would remember Sinai, where the twelve tribes received the covenant. Luke adds that Jesus spent the night before this choice in prayer (Luke 6:12).
str: v. 13: the call: he calls those he wants, and they come.
vv. 14–15: the purpose: to be with him, to be sent, to have authority.
vv. 16–19: the names, from Peter at the head to Judas at the end.
kw: The verb behind “appointed” is simply “he made” twelve. The group is not formed by the men's own decision. Twelve is the number of the tribes of Israel, and Jesus' action is a sign that God is gathering his people anew.
From apostellō, to send. An envoy who acts with the authority of the one who sends him. Some ancient manuscripts lack the words “whom he also named apostles” in v. 14, and the POC does not have them.
A name found only in Mark, explained by Mark himself. Its exact Aramaic form is uncertain. Luke 9:54 shows James and John ready to call down fire, which may give a hint of its meaning.
vv: He went up the mountain and called to him those whom he wanted, and they came to him.
The initiative is entirely his. Nothing is said of their merits. The whole of vocation lies in this one verse: he wants, he calls, they come.
And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message,
“To be with him” comes first. Those who are sent have nothing to carry except what they received by staying with him. The order still holds for every priest, catechist and parent.
and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
Every Gospel list of the Twelve puts Peter first and Judas last. The Church has never hidden this. Being chosen by Jesus is a gift, and it can be refused.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its teaching on the bishops with this passage: the Lord, having prayed to the Father, called to himself those he desired and appointed twelve (Lumen Gentium 19). The Catechism sees in the Twelve the Lord's emissaries, and in their sending the continuation of his own mission from the Father (CCC 858). With Peter at their head they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765).

qa: If the first covenant is “obsolete”, has God finished with the Jewish people?

No. Hebrews is comparing the old priesthood and sacrifices with the one sacrifice of Christ. It is not speaking about God's faithfulness to Israel. St Paul says of Israel: “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The Church teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121; see Nostra Aetate 4). Jeremiah's promise itself was made first to “the house of Israel and … the house of Judah”, and the first Christians were Jews who saw it fulfilled in Jesus.
study: Is God's law for me still mainly something outside me, or has it begun to be written on my heart? What would show the difference?
Jesus calls the Twelve first “to be with him”. How much of my service of God comes out of time spent with him?

lead: Today's two readings could hardly be more different in size, and they meet at the same point: what it costs Jesus to give himself. Hebrews shows the high priest entering the true sanctuary with his own blood. Mark, in two short verses, shows the crowds pressing so hard that he cannot eat, and his own family setting out to restrain him. Psalm 47, a song of God's enthronement which the Church also sings on the Ascension, stands between them.

r.h: Once for all, with his own blood
set: Hebrews is comparing the worship of the desert tent with what Christ has done. The tent had two rooms: the Holy Place, entered daily by the priests, and the Holy of Holies behind the second curtain, entered only by the high priest, once a year, with blood, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The Lectionary keeps the outline of the tent (vv. 2–3) and passes straight to Christ.
str: vv. 2–3: the two rooms of the tent.
vv. 11–12: Christ enters the greater tent with his own blood.
vv. 13–14: from the lesser to the greater: “how much more”.
kw: The word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tent of Exodus. The “greater and perfect tent” is not a building. Among the Fathers some saw it as the heavens through which Christ passed, others as his own body.
The high priest returned every year. Christ's sacrifice does not need repeating, because it is complete.
The old rites purified “the flesh” (v. 13). Hebrews says that Christ reaches the place no outward rite could reach, the inner person who knows himself before God.
vv: But when Christ came as a high priest of the good things that have come,

A note on the text: some of the oldest manuscripts read “that have come”, which the NRSV follows. Many others, and the Latin Vulgate, read “to come”, which the POC follows. Both are true to the faith: in Christ the good things have come, and their fullness is still ahead.
he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.
Priest and victim are one person. No one else in the old worship could say so.
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!

The argument runs through the ashes of the heifer (Numbers 19) to Christ. Most of the Fathers took “the eternal Spirit” to mean the Holy Spirit, so that the Trinity is at work in the Cross. Cleansing has a purpose: we are cleansed in order to worship.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ entered heaven itself as our high priest (CCC 662), and that the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross and is not another sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367). St John Chrysostom, preaching on Hebrews, says that we do not offer another sacrifice each day, but always the same one (in substance). This is why the Mass is never a repetition of Calvary, and why Catholics speak of taking part in it.

r.h: They went out to restrain him
set: These two verses open one of Mark's “sandwiches”, a story he begins, interrupts with another and then finishes. His family sets out here (vv. 20–21). Scribes from Jerusalem then accuse him of working by Beelzebul (vv. 22–30). His family arrives at the end (vv. 31–35). The two parts explain each other: even those closest to him do not yet understand who he is.
str: v. 20: the crowd again, so thick that there is no time to eat.
v. 21: his family hears and sets out, because of what is being said.
kw: Literally “those from him”. The phrase can mean relatives or close associates. The NRSV's “family” fits v. 31, where his mother and brothers arrive.
A strong word. Mark uses the same verb for the arrest of John the Baptist (6:17) and of Jesus himself (14:46).
From existēmi, to stand outside oneself. The Greek says only “they were saying”, so it is not clear who said it. The NRSV takes it as “people”. The POC takes it that the relatives had heard it said.
vv: and the crowd came together again, so that they could not even eat.
Mark returns to this detail at 6:31. The Son of God has an empty stomach and no time to himself. Love of people costs ordinary things.
When his family heard it, they went out to restrain him, for people were saying, “He has gone out of his mind.”

This is a human reaction: concern, embarrassment, perhaps fear for his life. A later writer would hardly have invented it, which is one reason many scholars take it as very old memory. St Paul knows the same charge: “if we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Corinthians 5:13).
ch: The Church's reading holds two things together. Jesus is true man, with a family, tired, misunderstood and unable to find a meal (CCC 470). And he is the one whom God sent, whose zeal looks like madness to the world. In the tradition of the saints that “madness” became a title of honour, drawn from St Paul: “We are fools for the sake of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4:10).

qa: Did Mary think her son had lost his mind?

The text does not say so. Mary is not named in these two verses; “his family” is a general term and v. 31 only says she came. John also records that “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5), and she is never said to have shared that. A mother who feared for her son's health would be natural. Luke presents her as the one who believed (Luke 1:45), and the Church teaches that her faith never wavered (CCC 149), though it was a real pilgrimage of faith (Lumen Gentium 58).
study: Hebrews says we are cleansed “to worship the living God”. What “dead works” keep me from worshipping him with my whole heart?
Have I ever been told that my faith was going too far? When was that person right, and when was it my faith that was right?

lead: On the Sunday of the Word of God, the readings show what a word from God does when someone hears it. It reaches Jonah “a second time”, and a pagan city turns round in a day. It comes from the lips of Jesus on a lakeshore, and four fishermen leave their nets. Psalm 25 is the prayer of everyone who has heard that word and wants to walk by it. St Paul adds the reason for haste: “the appointed time has grown short”. Mark uses the same Greek word for time, kairos, in the first words Jesus speaks in his Gospel. The key words today are turn, time and follow.

r.h: The word came a second time
set: The Book of Jonah is unlike the other prophetic books. It contains almost no oracles and is mostly a story about a prophet. A Jonah son of Amittai is mentioned at 2 Kings 14:25, in the eighth century BC, but most scholars date the book itself after the exile and read it as a teaching story, with its great fish and its city of huge size. The Church does not have to settle that question to receive its teaching, and Jesus himself draws on it (Matthew 12:40–41).

Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC. It fell in 612 BC. For Israel's memory it was the enemy. In chapter 1 Jonah ran away from this mission, and God brought him back. Today's reading skips vv. 6–9, the king's decree, and goes straight to God's answer. The book ends with God's question to the angry prophet: “should I not be concerned about Nineveh, that great city” (4:11).
str: vv. 1–2: the word comes a second time: the same command.
v. 3: this time Jonah goes. The size of the city.
v. 4: a sermon of five Hebrew words.
v. 5: the people believe, fast and put on sackcloth, “great and small”.
v. 10: God sees and changes his mind.
¶ Jonah does almost nothing. All the movement in this chapter comes from the word of God and from the people's response to it.
kw: Jonah's sermon is only five words in Hebrew. This last word comes from hāpak, the verb used of the overthrow of Sodom (Genesis 19:25). But the same verb can also mean to turn or to be changed. So the prophecy comes true in a way Jonah did not want: Nineveh is indeed turned over, by conversion.
The Old Testament's great word for repentance. It is a change of direction, not only of feeling. It appears in v. 8 and in v. 10: they “turned from their evil ways”.
to change one's mind, to relent
The same verb appears at Jeremiah 18:8, where God sets out the rule: if a nation turns from its evil, he will change his mind about the disaster. See the question below.
vv: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying,
God does not look for a better prophet. He repeats himself to the one who ran away. This is the mercy of the second chance, given before Nineveh ever gets hers.
Now Nineveh was an exceedingly large city, a three days’ walk across.

Literally “a great city to God”, a Hebrew idiom for something very great. The reader may also hear in it a hint of what the book will say at the end: this city matters to God. Nineveh, large as it was, could be crossed in much less than three days. The story's language is larger than life.
And he cried out, “Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!”
Forty is the Bible's number for a time of testing: the flood, Sinai, the desert. The sermon has no call to repent, no promise and no name of God.
And the people of Nineveh believed God; they proclaimed a fast, and everyone, great and small, put on sackcloth.
“Believed” is the verb used of Abraham (Genesis 15:6). Pagans do at once what the prophet of God had refused to do.
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways, God changed his mind about the calamity that he had said he would bring upon them; and he did not do it.
Note what God sees. The verse does not mention the fast or the sackcloth, but “what they did”: they turned from evil.
ch: Jesus holds up Nineveh as a judgment on those who hear him and do not turn: “they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!” (Matthew 12:41). St John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch, makes the point of v. 10 again and again: it was not the fast by itself that saved the city, but the change of life (in substance). The Catechism says the same: the call to conversion does not aim first at outward works, “sackcloth and ashes”, but at the conversion of the heart (CCC 1430). The Roman Lectionary also reads this chapter in the first week of Lent.

r.h: Make me to know your ways
set: Psalm 25 is an alphabetical poem: its verses begin, with a few irregularities, with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order. It is a personal prayer of someone under pressure, who is aware of past sin and who asks above all for guidance. It suits today's readings exactly, since the people of Nineveh have just left their “evil ways” and now need another way to walk in.
str: vv. 4–5: teach me your ways.
vv. 6–7: remember your mercy, and do not remember my sins.
vv. 8–9: the Lord teaches sinners and the humble.
¶ The first half speaks to God and the last part speaks about God. A prayer for guidance becomes a confession that God does guide.
kw: A road, then a way of life. The word appears in v. 4 and v. 8, and again in v. 9. The early Christians would be called followers of “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
God's faithful, covenant love. Together with mercy in v. 6 it echoes God's self-description at Exodus 34:6.
Verses 6–7 play on this word. Remember your mercy, do not remember my sins, remember me. To be remembered by God means to be held in his love (compare Luke 23:42).
vv: Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths.
Today's response takes up this verse. It is a beggar's prayer. The psalmist does not claim to know the road.
Do not remember the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for your goodness’ sake, O Lord!
The ground of the request is not the sinner's goodness but God's.
Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way.
“Therefore” is the surprise of the verse. Because God is upright, one might expect him to punish. Instead he teaches. Jonah 4:2 will complain of this very thing.
ch: The Catechism calls the Psalms the masterwork of prayer in the Old Testament (CCC 2585). Sung between Jonah and the Gospel, this psalm puts into the mouth of the people at Mass the same turning that the Ninevites made and the same willingness to be led that the fishermen showed. Every Christian who prays it is asking to become a disciple.

r.h: The present form of this world is passing away
set: St Paul writes to the Church in Corinth from Ephesus (16:8), about AD 53–55. In chapter 7 he answers questions the Corinthians have sent him on marriage and celibacy (7:1). He speaks in view of “the impending crisis” (7:26), and his sentences are shaped by the expectation that the Lord's coming is near. These three verses are not a set of rules. They state the outlook from which all the rest is to be read.
str: v. 29a: the statement: the time has grown short.
vv. 29b–31a: five examples of “as though not”: wives, mourning, rejoicing, buying, dealing with the world.
v. 31b: the reason: this world's form is passing away.
kw: Not time as it passes on a clock, but the moment God has decisively set. The same word as in today's Gospel (Mark 1:15).
A participle meaning drawn together, compressed. Since Christ came, time has a new shape: it presses toward its end.

The little phrase Paul repeats five times. It does not tell people to stop being married or to stop grieving. It tells them to hold everything in this world with open hands, because nothing here is ultimate.
The world as it now appears and is arranged. Paul does not say that the world is evil, only that its present form does not last.
vv: I mean, brothers and sisters, the appointed time has grown short; from now on, let even those who have wives be as though they had none,

Taken alone this could sound shocking. Paul has just told married couples not to deprive one another (7:5), and he recognises that a married person must care how to please the spouse (7:33). His point concerns what is ultimate, and it is not neglect of a spouse.
and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing,
Grief and joy are both real, and neither one is final. The Christian does not grieve “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and rejoices knowing that greater joy is coming.
For the present form of this world is passing away.
This sentence gives the reason. It is also a word of consolation for those for whom this world's form has been cruel.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up this verse. The form of this world, distorted by sin, is passing away, but God is preparing a new dwelling and a new earth. And the Council adds that this hope must make us care more about this earth, not less (Gaudium et Spes 39; CCC 1048–1049). The Catechism also teaches that marriage and virginity for the Kingdom both come from the Lord, and that they support one another (CCC 1620).

set: These are the first words and the first actions of Jesus' public ministry in Mark. They follow directly on his baptism and his forty days in the wilderness (1:9–13). Mark has no infancy story and no long preparation. John is “arrested” and Jesus begins.

Simon, Andrew, James and John fish on the Sea of Galilee, which is a freshwater lake. Fishing there was a real trade. Zebedee has “hired men” (v. 20), so these are not destitute people. They are leaving something.
str: vv. 14–15: Jesus' whole message in one sentence.
vv. 16–18: Simon and Andrew called; they leave the nets.
vv. 19–20: James and John called; they leave their father.
kw: The verb behind “arrested” (v. 14). Mark will use it again for Jesus (9:31; 14:41) and for his disciples (13:9). John's path already shows what the Gospel will cost.
Literally “change your mind”. The Hebrew idea of turning (šûb) stands behind it. The Greek is a present imperative, which can suggest a turning that goes on.
In the Roman world this word was used for announcements of imperial victories and birthdays. Mark uses it of God's own coming to reign.
Literally “come after me”. Jewish students usually chose their own teacher. Here the teacher chooses, and what he asks is not first to learn a doctrine but to walk behind him.
vv: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news.
Two statements of fact and two commands, and the order matters. God's action comes first: the time is full, the Kingdom is near. Repentance is the answer to good news, not the price of it.
And Jesus said to them, “Follow me and I will make you fish for people.”
He takes up their own trade. Grace does not throw away what they know. Jeremiah 16:16 used fishers as an image of judgment; here the catch is a rescue.
And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
“Immediately” (euthys) is Mark's favourite word. No conversation, no question, no explanation. Compare the people of Nineveh: the word comes, and they act.
Immediately he called them; and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, and followed him.
Mark leaves the picture standing: an old man in a boat with his workers, watching his two sons go. The call has a human cost, and the Gospel does not hide it. See the question below.
ch: The Catechism places Mark 1:14–15 at the opening of its teaching on the Kingdom (CCC 541) and on conversion: it is the first call that Christ makes (CCC 1427). St Gregory the Great, preaching on the calling of Peter and Andrew, asks what these poor men left who had so little. He answers that we must weigh the love more than the amount: the one who holds nothing back for himself has given up much (in substance). The Lectionary reads Mark in this Year B, so this is the opening of the Gospel the Church will walk with for most of the year.

qa: Can God change his mind? Is he not unchangeable?

God's being and his will to save do not change. Scripture uses human language: “God changed his mind” tells us that God's threats are a call, not a fixed sentence. Jeremiah 18:8 makes this the rule: if a nation turns, God will not bring the disaster. What has changed in Jonah 3 is Nineveh. The same God who threatened in order to save goes on saving.
Must Catholics believe that Jonah's story happened exactly as told?

The Church teaches that to understand Scripture we must attend to its literary forms (Dei Verbum 12; CCC 110). Many Catholic scholars read Jonah as an inspired teaching story, and others have read it as history. In either case what it teaches is God's truth: his mercy reaches beyond Israel, and it asks a change of heart from all of us. Jesus' use of the story to speak of his own Resurrection is not affected by this question.
Does Jesus want people to abandon their parents and families?

No. Jesus himself rebukes those who use religion to avoid caring for their parents (Mark 7:10–13). But he does ask that the bond with him come before every other bond (CCC 1618). What he asks differs from one person to another. To some he says “Follow me” with their feet; to others, like the man healed at Gerasa, he says “Go home to your friends” (Mark 5:19). Each is a true disciple.
rite: In the Roman Rite this is the Sunday of the Word of God, set by Pope Francis in Aperuit illis (2019), which asks that this Sunday be given to the celebration, study and spreading of God's word. The Pope noted that it falls when the Church strengthens her bonds with the Jewish people and prays for Christian unity. In the Roman Lectionary the first reading on these Sundays is chosen to fit the Gospel, while the second reading runs on through a letter, which is why St Paul's words on the time join the others in their own way. This year the memorial of St Francis de Sales, patron of Catholic writers, is not kept because it falls on Sunday. St Jerome's saying fits the day well: ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ (Dei Verbum 25; CCC 133).
study: God speaks to Jonah “a second time”. What word have I run away from, and has it come to me again?
The Ninevites turned at a sermon of five words. What keeps me from turning after a lifetime of sermons?
Paul says to hold everything “as though not”. What in my life do I hold too tightly, as if it would last for ever?
The fishermen left their nets. What are my “nets”? In the place where I now live and work, what does “Follow me” ask of me this week?

lead: The Church keeps today the moment that turned a persecutor into an apostle. In the first reading Paul tells the story himself, in his own defence, on the steps of the Temple area in Jerusalem. The psalm, the shortest in the Psalter, calls all nations to praise, and Paul himself will quote it. The Gospel gives the command which that meeting on the road placed on his shoulders: “Go into all the world.” The feast also closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. The key words are way, witness and all.

r.h: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?
set: Acts tells this story three times: in Luke's own narrative (9:1–22), and twice in Paul's speeches (22:3–16; 26:9–18). This repetition shows how much the event matters to Luke. Today's text is the first of the two speeches. Paul has just been seized after a disturbance in the Temple area and taken into Roman custody (21:27–36). The tribune allows him to speak, and he addresses the crowd “in the Hebrew language” (21:40), most probably Aramaic. So he tells the story as a Jew speaking to fellow Jews.

Where Acts 9:1–22 is chosen instead, the same events are told from outside. It adds the Lord's word to Ananias: “he is an instrument whom I have chosen” (9:15). It also tells of Paul's three days of blindness and of his first preaching in the synagogues of Damascus.
str: vv. 3–5: Paul's past: a Jew, a pupil of Gamaliel, a zealous persecutor.
vv. 6–11: the road: the light, the voice, the two questions, the blindness.
vv. 12–16: Ananias: sight restored, a mission given, Baptism.
kw: Paul honours his hearers by saying that they are zealous for God as he was. Zeal is good, and it can go tragically wrong. He gives the same account of himself at Galatians 1:14 and Philippians 3:6.
An early name for the Christian movement (9:2; 19:9; 24:14). It describes faith as a road to be walked, more than a set of opinions.

Ananias says Paul will be a witness “of what you have seen and heard” (v. 15). Luke uses the same word for the Twelve (1:8), and here Paul receives the same task. The word later came to mean a martyr.
vv: I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated strictly according to our ancestral law, being zealous for God, just as all of you are today.

Paul speaks in the present tense: “I am a Jew”. To sit at someone's feet was the posture of a pupil. Gamaliel is the honoured teacher of the law who counselled moderation at 5:34. Paul does not renounce his people or their God. Later he asks, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1).
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’

The name is doubled, as when God calls Abraham (Genesis 22:11) and Moses (Exodus 3:4). And the question has a startling word in it: “me”. Saul thinks he is arresting men and women. Jesus says that what is done to them is done to him.
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ Then he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth whom you are persecuting.’
“Lord” here may first be simply a reverent address. Then the answer comes. The whole of Paul's later theology of the Body of Christ can be found in this short exchange.
I asked, ‘What am I to do, Lord?’

The second question is the true beginning of conversion. Saul had always known what to do. The answer is not given by the voice from heaven. He must go to the city and be told by someone in the Church.
A certain Ananias, who was a devout man according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,

Speaking to this audience, Paul describes Ananias by his Jewish piety (at 9:10 Luke calls him “a disciple”). The one who restores Paul's sight is a Jew faithful to the law. Ananias's greeting is one of the most moving words in Acts: “Brother Saul” (v. 13).
And now why do you delay? Get up, be baptized, and have your sins washed away, calling on his name.
The great light does not replace the sacrament. Even Paul is baptized by another. “Calling on his name” is what Christians are known for (9:14), and it echoes Joel's promise (Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21).
ch: The Catechism teaches that all sins are forgiven by Baptism (CCC 1263), and it sees in Paul's words about his calling the Christian confession of Jesus as the Son of God (CCC 442; Galatians 1:15–16). St Augustine loved the words “why are you persecuting me”. The head in heaven cries out for the members on earth, he says, and so Christ and his Church are one (in substance). This is the root of the Church's teaching on the Body of Christ (CCC 787–795). St John Chrysostom, who preached seven homilies in Paul's praise, says that what made Paul was his love for Christ, which he prized above all things (in substance).

r.h: Praise the Lord, all you nations
set: Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm in the Bible, only two verses. It belongs to the group of Psalms 113–118, the Hallel, sung at the great Jewish feasts and especially at Passover. Many scholars think that the hymn Jesus and his disciples sang after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26) came from this group. The response today comes from the Gospel: “Go out to all the world and tell the good news.”
str: v. 1: the call: all nations, all peoples.
v. 2: the reason: God's love and faithfulness.
kw: The word usually means the non-Israelite peoples. Israel's own praise calls them to join in.
God's covenant love. The nations are called to praise God for what he has done “toward us”, that is, for his love of Israel.
That which holds firm and can be relied on. With ḥesed it forms one of the Bible's great pairs of words about God.
vv: Praise the Lord, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!

St Paul quotes this verse at Romans 15:11, in the Greek wording, in his argument that Gentiles and Jews together are to glorify God. So the apostle of the Gentiles found his mission already sung in the Psalter.
For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the Lord endures forever. Praise the Lord!
“Great” here translates a verb of strength: his love prevails. The two verses say in small what Paul lived: God's faithfulness to Israel is good news for all peoples.
ch: Sung on this feast, the psalm reads as a commentary on Paul's life. The Church reads it as a sign that God's plan always included the nations, and she teaches that all peoples are called to the one People of God (CCC 831; Lumen Gentium 13). It is short enough for anyone to learn by heart.

set: These verses belong to the “longer ending” of Mark (16:9–20). The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, end the Gospel at 16:8, and many scholars think the longer ending was added by another hand, drawing on the other Gospels and on Acts. But it is very old: St Irenaeus knew it in the second century. The Council of Trent received the books of Scripture entire, “with all their parts”, and the Church reads these verses as inspired Scripture, whoever wrote them.
The Church chooses this reading today because it describes what happened in Paul. Most of what is promised in vv. 17–18 can be found in the Acts of the Apostles, and much of it in Paul's own story.
str: v. 15: the command: everywhere, to everyone.
v. 16: the response: faith and Baptism, or refusal.
vv. 17–18: the signs that go with those who believe.
kw: To announce as a herald. The herald does not create the message and does not debate it. He says what the king has done.
Not only “all people” but “the whole creation”. Compare Paul at Colossians 1:23 and Romans 8:19–22, where all creation is waiting.
Not displays of power for their own sake but pointers: they show who is at work in the proclamation.
vv: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
This verse gives the feast its Gospel. The man who said “Who are you, Lord?” spent the rest of his life doing this, from Damascus to Rome.
The one who believes and is baptized will be saved; but the one who does not believe will be condemned.
See the question below. Faith and Baptism go together, just as in Ananias's words to Paul.
And these signs will accompany those who believe: by using my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues;
Acts shows these things: demons cast out by Paul (16:18), tongues at Ephesus when he lays hands on new believers (19:6).
they will pick up snakes in their hands, and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.
Paul is bitten by a viper on Malta and “suffered no harm” (Acts 28:5). He then heals the father of Publius by laying his hands on him (Acts 28:8).
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses on Baptism and faith (CCC 977, 1257), and on the Church's ministry to the sick, which the risen Lord confirms through signs done in his name (CCC 1507). It also grounds the whole missionary work of the Church in the Lord's command (CCC 849–851). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is by her very nature missionary (Ad Gentes 2).

qa: Did Saul change his name to Paul at his conversion?

No, this is a common mistake. Acts goes on calling him Saul for several chapters after Damascus, and then says “Saul, also known as Paul” (13:9). Saul is his Hebrew name, and Paul is the Roman name he uses in the Greek-speaking world. Many Jews of the time had two such names. What changed on the road was his life, not his name.
Did those with Paul hear the voice or not? Acts 9:7 and 22:9 seem to differ.

Acts 9:7 says they heard the voice but saw no one. Acts 22:9 says they saw the light but did not hear the voice. Luke wrote both and kept both, so he does not see a contradiction. Some explain that they heard a sound but could not make out the words. In both accounts the point is the same: the others knew something happened, but only Paul received the message.
What about “the one who does not believe will be condemned”? Are those who have never heard lost?

The verse speaks of someone who has truly heard the Gospel and refuses it. The Church teaches that faith and Baptism are necessary for salvation for those to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed (CCC 161, 1257), and also that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, may attain eternal salvation (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). The mission remains urgent, because it brings people the joy of knowing Christ.
Should Christians handle snakes as a test of faith?

No. The verse promises protection to messengers in danger, as with Paul at Malta. It does not command anyone to seek danger. Jesus refused to throw himself from the Temple, saying, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7).
rite: In the Roman Rite today's feast has its Gloria, and it closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. The General Roman Calendar keeps no other saint's conversion as a feast. The closing of the week on this day is fitting. Paul asked the divided Corinthians, “Has Christ been divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:13), and the man who once wanted to bind the Church came to spend his life for her unity. Popes usually close the week with Vespers at the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls in Rome. Today every parish may pray for the unity of all Christians, and pray with respect for the Jewish people, Paul's own people, whom he never stopped loving (Romans 9:3–5).
study: Paul had zeal for God and was still wrong. Where might my own zeal be blinding me, and how could I test it?
Jesus says “me” of those Saul persecutes. How does this change the way I treat the least of the members of the Church?
Paul needed Ananias to tell him what to do. Who has been an Ananias for me? For whom might I be one?
“Go into all the world”: what is my part in this command in the place where I live?

lead: The day after the feast of St Paul, the Church remembers two of the men he trained. Paul's letter to Timothy speaks of a faith handed down by a grandmother and a mother, and then by an apostle's hands. In the Gospel Jesus looks at those sitting around him and names a family made by doing God's will. Blood and baptism, home and Church: the two readings together show how faith is passed on.

set: Timothy came from Lystra in Asia Minor, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1–3). He became Paul's closest companion: “how like a son with a father he has served with me” (Philippians 2:22). Titus, a Greek (Galatians 2:3), was Paul's trusted envoy in the hard dealings with Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6–7). Church tradition, recorded by Eusebius, names Timothy first bishop of Ephesus and Titus first bishop of Crete.

This letter presents itself as Paul's last words, from prison. Many modern scholars think the letters to Timothy and Titus were written by a follower in Paul's name, while others hold that Paul wrote them, perhaps through a secretary. Either way the Church receives them as inspired Scripture. If Titus 1:1–5 is read instead, its point is the setting of elders in each town, the ordering of a young Church.
str: vv. 1–2: greeting to a beloved child.
vv. 3–5: remembrance: tears, prayers, the faith of three generations.
vv. 6–7: rekindle the gift given by the laying on of hands.
v. 8: do not be ashamed; join in suffering.
kw: Literally to stir a fire back into flame. The gift has not gone out, but embers need to be stirred. The word occurs only here in the New Testament.
Here the grace of ministry, given “through the laying on of my hands”. Compare 1 Timothy 4:14, which names also the council of elders.
A sound and steady mind. It is the opposite of panic. With power and love it completes the description of the Spirit in v. 7.
vv: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, lives in you.

Two women are named here, the two through whom faith first reached a future bishop. Compare 3:15: “from childhood you have known the sacred writings”. Many readers of these words have thought of their own grandmothers. The home comes before the seminary.
For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands;
Ordination does not wear out, yet it does need tending. St John Chrysostom notes that as fire needs fuel, so grace needs our eagerness (in substance).
for God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but rather a spirit of power and of love and of self-discipline.
Timothy seems to have been a shy man (compare 1 Corinthians 16:10–11). Paul does not tell him to change his nature. He reminds him of what has been given.
ch: The Catechism draws on these very verses and on Titus 1:5 in its teaching on Holy Orders: Paul's words to Timothy and Titus show the apostolic laying on of hands and the ordering of ministers in the Church (CCC 1590). It teaches too that the family is the first school of faith, the domestic Church (CCC 1656–1657).

r.h: Here are my mother and my brothers
set: This passage closes the “sandwich” Mark opened at 3:20–21: his family set out to restrain him, scribes accused him (3:22–30), and now his mother and brothers arrive. There are two circles in the scene. Those “outside” stand and send a message. Those inside are “sitting around him”, the posture of disciples.
str: vv. 31–32: the family outside; the message comes in.
v. 33: Jesus' question.
vv. 34–35: the look and the answer.
kw: A word in Greek, as in Hebrew and Aramaic, that can extend to relatives of various kinds. See the question below.
A favourite verb of Mark for the look of Jesus (3:5; 5:32; 10:23). He takes time to see each face.
The one condition of this family. Compare the prayer in Gethsemane: “not what I want, but what you want” (14:36).
vv: And he replied, “Who are my mother and my brothers?”
The question is startling. It is not a rejection of his mother. It opens a family wider than blood.
And looking at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers!
In that society family was the strongest of bonds. He now gives that honour to the ordinary listeners around him.
Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.
He adds “sister”. No father is named here; the disciple's Father is God (compare 11:25).
ch: Who did the will of God more perfectly than Mary? St Augustine says it was a greater thing for her to be Christ's disciple than to be his mother (in substance). The Council teaches that she received these words as one who was faithfully keeping God's word (Lumen Gentium 58). The Catechism applies v. 35 to all who enter God's family (CCC 2233).

qa: Did Mary have other children, since Mark speaks of Jesus' brothers and sisters?

The Church teaches that Mary remained ever virgin (CCC 499–501). The Bible's word for brothers has a wide range: Abraham calls his nephew Lot his “brother” (Genesis 13:8 in the Hebrew). Matthew names James and Joseph among the brothers of Jesus (13:55), and later speaks of “Mary the mother of James and Joseph” (27:56), another Mary who was a disciple (CCC 500). St Jerome took these brothers to be cousins. An ancient Eastern tradition held they were children of Joseph from an earlier marriage. Many other Christians read the words differently, and the Church teaches her faith with respect for them.
rite: Saints Timothy and Titus are kept as a memorial in the Roman Rite, placed by the 1969 calendar directly after the feast of St Paul, whose helpers they were. In India this date is also Republic Day. Where the bishops permit, the Mass for the Nation may be used. St Paul himself asks that prayers be made “for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:2). On this day we pray for all the people of the nation and for those who serve them.
study: Who first gave me my faith? Have I thanked God for them, and whom am I handing it on to?
What gift of God in me has burned low? What would it take to rekindle it this week?

lead: Two things that seem opposite stand side by side today. Hebrews says that Christ's work is finished: one offering, and he has sat down. Mark says that the word is still being sown, and that much depends on the ground it falls on. The two belong together. What Christ has done is complete and cannot be repeated, while our receiving of it takes a lifetime. The key words are single, word and hear. Psalm 110, the psalm of the day, is the very text Hebrews leans on when it speaks of Christ seated at God's right hand.

r.h: He sat down: one offering, complete
set: This passage closes the long central argument of Hebrews about Christ the high priest (chapters 7–10). The author has compared the sacrifices of the old covenant with the offering of Christ, and now he gathers the whole argument into one picture: a priest who stands and a priest who sits.
str: vv. 11–14: two pictures. Every priest stands day after day; Christ offers once and sits down.
vv. 15–18: the witness of the Holy Spirit in Jeremiah 31: the law written within, and sins remembered no more.
kw: Hebrews uses the word “offering” for the whole gift of Christ's life and death. “Single” is the point of the sentence: nothing needs to be added to it.

The Greek perfect tense speaks of a finished act whose effect remains. “Those who are sanctified” (v. 14) is a present participle and may also be read “those who are being sanctified”. The work is done; its effect is still reaching us.
vv: And every priest stands day after day at his service, offering again and again the same sacrifices that can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, “he sat down at the right hand of God,”
The contrast is in the posture. To stand is to be still on duty. To sit is to have finished, and at God's right hand it is also to reign. The words come from Psalm 110:1.
For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified.
This verse holds both sides of the Christian life: what Christ has done once, and what is still happening in us.
“I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”
Hebrews quoted the whole of Jeremiah's promise in chapter 8 (8:8–12) and now recalls only its two central lines. The new covenant reaches the heart, and God's forgiveness is complete.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the redemptive sacrifice of Christ is unique, accomplished once for all, and yet made present in the Eucharistic sacrifice of the Church (CCC 1545). So the Mass does not add to the Cross or repeat it. As the Council of Trent says, the victim is one and the same, and only the manner of offering is different (CCC 1367). When we read of the old sacrifices we remember that Hebrews is a Christian preacher's argument about Christ, and that the Church honours God's covenant with Israel, which was never revoked (CCC 121, 839).

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: This is the first long block of Jesus' teaching in Mark (4:1–34). Chapter 3 has shown that people respond to him in very different ways, some with faith and some with suspicion. Now Jesus sits in a boat, in the posture of a teacher, with the crowd on the shore, and he tells a story that explains why the same word has such different results.
str: vv. 1–2: the scene by the sea.
vv. 3–9: the parable, framed by “Listen!” and “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
vv. 10–12: why parables: the words of Isaiah.
vv. 13–20: the explanation, soil by soil.
kw: It renders the Hebrew māshāl, which can mean a comparison, a proverb or a riddle. A parable teaches, and it also makes the hearer think and decide.
This is the only time Mark uses the word. It is not a piece of hidden knowledge. It is God's plan, which is now being opened in Jesus himself.
Literally “they are made to stumble” (v. 17). The word for the rocky ground is the same word Jesus later uses for the disciples on the night of his arrest (14:27).
vv: “Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The first word of the parable is a command. Everything in this chapter turns on how we hear.
Other seed fell into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.”

Three kinds of loss are followed by three kinds of harvest. A hundredfold is the harvest of Isaac in Genesis 26:12, a mark of God's blessing. The sower is not discouraged by the waste. The harvest is greater than the losses.
but the cares of the world, and the lure of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it yields nothing.
The thorns are the most ordinary danger of all. No one here rejects the word. It is simply crowded out.
ch: St Gregory the Great, preaching on this parable, remarks that no one would have believed him had he dared to call riches thorns, but the Lord himself does so, because they prick the soul with care (in substance). The Second Vatican Council says that the Church receives the bread of life from the one table of the word of God and the Body of Christ (Dei Verbum 21). Each Mass is therefore a sowing, and the homily and the silence after it are part of the care of the soil.

qa: Does Jesus use parables so that people will not understand and be forgiven (4:12)?

He is quoting Isaiah 6:9–10, where God sends the prophet to a people who will refuse to hear. The Bible often speaks of a sad result as if it were part of God's purpose, since nothing lies outside his plan. It does not mean that God wishes anyone to be lost. The Catechism explains that the parables invite everyone to the feast of the Kingdom and also ask for a choice; to those who stay “outside”, everything remains a riddle (CCC 546). The disciples do not understand either, and they are not rejected. They stay close and ask.
study: Hebrews 10:14 says that Christ “has perfected” and that we are “sanctified”. Where do I live as if the Cross were not yet enough?
Which soil describes me this week, and what is the thorn that most often crowds out the word?

lead: On the memorial of St Thomas Aquinas, the readings speak of two things he gave his life to: drawing near to God, and passing on the light. Hebrews turns from teaching to encouragement, inviting us to approach, to hold fast, and to stir one another up. Mark asks a simple question about a lamp: who would hide it? The key words are approach, lamp and measure.

set: The word “Therefore” marks a turning point. The long argument about Christ's priesthood is finished, and from here the author draws out what it means for daily life. The sanctuary that only the high priest could enter, once a year, is now open.
str: vv. 19–21: what we have: confidence, a way, a great priest.
vv. 22–25: three exhortations: “let us approach” (faith), “let us hold fast” (hope), “let us consider” (love).
kw: Literally freedom of speech, the boldness of a citizen who may speak openly. Here it is the boldness of those who may come before God.
The veil before the Holy of Holies. Mark uses the same word when the curtain of the temple is torn at Jesus' death (Mark 15:38).
A strong word. In Acts 15:39 it is the “sharp” disagreement of Paul and Barnabas. Here the same energy is turned to stirring one another up to love.
vv: by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (that is, through his flesh),
The way into God's presence is not a road or a rule, but the humanity of Jesus, offered and risen.
let us approach with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.

These words recall the washing and sprinkling of priests (Exodus 29:4, 21) and the promise of clean water in Ezekiel 36:25. Many commentators hear in them a reference to baptism, which opens the way for every Christian.
not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another,
Even in the first generation some were staying away. The word used here for meeting (episynagōgē) means a gathering together.
ch: The Catechism cites this very passage when it teaches about the Sunday assembly: the custom of Christians gathering goes back to the beginnings of the apostolic age (CCC 2178). Faith, hope and love here are not ideas but three movements: toward God, in steadfastness, and toward one another. St Thomas Aquinas, who lectured on Hebrews, knew that the whole of theology exists for this approach to God.

set: These short sayings follow the explanation of the sower and continue its theme. Jesus has just said that the secret is given to those who stay with him. Now he says that what is given in secret is meant to shine.
str: vv. 21–23: the lamp: nothing is hidden except to be disclosed.
vv. 24–25: the measure: how we hear decides what we receive.
kw: A dry measure of about nine litres, a Latin word in Greek dress. A lamp under it would simply go out.
Elsewhere this saying is about judging others. Here Mark applies it to hearing: the attention we give is the measure of what we receive.
vv: He said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand?
The Greek says literally “Does the lamp come…”. Some commentators see here a hint that Jesus himself is the light who has come. Either way, the disciples are not given light for themselves alone.
And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear; the measure you give will be the measure you get, and still more will be given you.
The Greek is vivid: “See what you hear.” The passive “will be given” is a reverent way of saying that God gives, and he gives beyond the measure.
For to those who have, more will be given; and from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away.”
It sounds unjust if taken as a rule about money. In this chapter it is about hearing. The one who receives the word grows in understanding; the one who neglects it loses even what he had heard.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its teaching on the Church with this image: Christ is the light of the nations, and that light shines on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1). St Thomas Aquinas gave the lamp a famous expression. As it is greater to give light than only to shine, he says, so it is greater to hand on to others what one has contemplated than only to contemplate (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 188, a. 6, in substance).

qa: Why is it “unfair” that more is given to the one who has?

It is not a rule about possessions. In Mark 4 the one who “has” is the one who has listened. Anyone who has learned a language or a trade knows the same thing: what we use grows, and what we neglect fades.
rite: St Thomas Aquinas (about 1225–1274) was an Italian Dominican friar, priest and Doctor of the Church. His Summa Theologiae remained unfinished at his death, and tradition credits him with the texts of the Mass and Office of Corpus Christi, among them the Pange lingua. The date of his memorial, 28 January, recalls the transfer of his relics to Toulouse in 1369. He is a fitting patron for teachers, catechists and students.
study: Hebrews 10:24 asks us to “provoke one another to love and good deeds”. Whom could I encourage this week, and how?
What have I received in prayer or in study that I have kept under a basket?

lead: Both readings teach patience, each in its own way. Hebrews asks a tired community to look back at the courage of its first days and to look ahead to the Lord who will not delay. Jesus speaks of a seed that grows while the sower sleeps, and of the tiny mustard seed that shelters the birds. What God has begun, God will bring to harvest. The key words are endurance, of itself and smallest.

set: After a severe warning (10:26–31), the author changes his tone and recalls what these Christians have already come through. We do not know for certain who they were or which persecution he means. They seem to have suffered public shame, imprisonment and the loss of goods, though not yet death (see 12:4).
str: vv. 32–34: remember: the earlier days of struggle.
vv. 35–36: therefore do not abandon your confidence; you need endurance.
vv. 37–39: the Scripture and the conclusion: “we are not among those who shrink back”.
kw: A word from the athletic contest, found only here in the New Testament. Christian life is pictured as a long contest (compare 12:1).
From the word for theatre: they were made a public spectacle.
Not passive waiting, but staying under a burden and holding on.
vv: But recall those earlier days when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,
“Enlightened” is the same word as in 6:4. By the second century St Justin Martyr calls baptism “enlightenment” (First Apology 61). Remembering the grace of our beginnings is a way to stay faithful.
and you cheerfully accepted the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you yourselves possessed something better and more lasting.
Their joy did not come from pretending that the loss meant nothing. It came from knowing what could not be taken.
but my righteous one will live by faith. My soul takes no pleasure in anyone who shrinks back.”

Hebrews quotes Habakkuk 2:3–4 in its Greek form, with a phrase from Isaiah 26:20. St Paul uses the same line of Habakkuk in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11. Here it speaks of the faith that perseveres through trial.
ch: The Catechism teaches that to live, grow and persevere in the faith until the end we must nourish it with the word of God and beg the Lord to increase it (CCC 162). Tertullian said that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50, in substance), a saying that fits today's Gospel well. In many lands today there are Christians and others who suffer loss for their conscience. We pray for them, and for those who have wronged them.

r.h: The seed grows, he does not know how
set: These are the last parables of the discourse by the sea. The first, the seed growing by itself, is found only in Mark. The second, the mustard seed, is also in Matthew 13 and Luke 13. Jesus' hearers could see how small his following was and how powerful his opponents, and these parables speak to that.
str: vv. 26–29: the seed that grows by itself, and the harvest.
vv. 30–32: the mustard seed and the large shrub.
vv. 33–34: a summary of Jesus' way of teaching.
kw: The source of our word “automatic”. It does not mean that the seed needs no sowing or soil. It means that the growth comes from a power the farmer does not control.
The mustard seed was a proverbial image of smallness. The plant can grow taller than a person, but it remains a garden shrub, not a cedar. Jesus chooses a humble image on purpose.
Birds nesting in great trees is an Old Testament image for a kingdom that shelters the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12).
vv: and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
The farmer is not lazy. He has sown, and he will reap. But he cannot make the grain grow, and he need not lose sleep over it.
But when the grain is ripe, at once he goes in with his sickle, because the harvest has come.”
The words echo Joel 3:13, a picture of God's judgment. Patience is not the absence of an end. The harvest will come.
yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes the greatest of all shrubs, and puts forth large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.”
The smallest beginning, Jesus and a few fishermen in Galilee, is already the Kingdom in seed.
ch: The Second Vatican Council draws on these parables: those who hear the word with faith and join the little flock of Christ have received the Kingdom itself, and then by its own power the seed sprouts and grows until the harvest (Lumen Gentium 5). St Gregory the Great, in his homilies on Ezekiel, applies the parable to the soul: we sow by a good intention, we sleep by resting in hope, and the seed grows beyond what we can see (in substance).

qa: Is the mustard seed really the smallest seed on earth?

There are smaller seeds. Jesus is not teaching botany. He uses a common saying of his people, for whom the mustard seed was the very picture of something tiny. The point is the contrast between the beginning and the end.
study: What grace from the beginning of my faith do I need to remember today (Hebrews 10:32)?
Where do I need to stop trying to control the growth, and trust that God is at work while I sleep?

lead: Today's question is what faith looks like when one cannot see the way. Abraham sets out “not knowing where he was going”. The disciples, in a boat full of water, wake the sleeping Jesus and ask whether he cares. Between the two readings the Church sings the canticle of Zechariah, which recalls “the oath that he swore to our ancestor Abraham”. The key words are assurance, stranger and faith. The question Jesus asks in the boat is the question Hebrews answers.

set: Chapter 11 is the great roll-call of the faith of Israel's ancestors. It answers the last line of chapter 10: “we are… among those who have faith”. Abel, Enoch and Noah (vv. 3–7) are left out today, and the reading goes straight to Abraham and Sarah, to whom Hebrews gives more space than to anyone else. The story behind it is told in Genesis 12–22.
str: vv. 1–2: what faith is.
vv. 8–10: Abraham sets out and lives in tents, looking for a city.
vv. 11–12: descendants from one who was “as good as dead”.
vv. 13–16: they died without receiving the promises: strangers seeking a homeland.
vv. 17–19: the offering of Isaac.
kw: The word can mean a foundation or substance, and the Latin renders it substantia. Benedict XVI explains that faith already gives us something of what we hope for, so that the future reaches into the present (Spe Salvi 7).
Also “proof” or “testing”. Faith is a way of being sure about what is not seen.
“In a parable” (v. 19), the same word as the parables of Mark 4. Isaac's return is a figure of something greater.
vv: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.
The Catechism says that Abraham fulfils this definition of faith (CCC 146). It is less a definition for the classroom than a description of how the ancestors lived.
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
He obeys first and understands later. The Greek word for “obeyed” is built on the word for hearing.
By faith he received power of procreation, even though he was too old

A note on the text. The Greek of this verse is difficult. The NRSV makes Abraham the subject and treats Sarah's barrenness as a side remark. Other translations, and the Malayalam POC, make Sarah the subject. Either way, both are past hope, and God keeps his word.
They confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth,
They lived in the promised land as guests. The Letter to Diognetus (5) says the same of Christians: every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland is foreign to them (in substance).
He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead
Hebrews reads Genesis 22 in the light of Easter. Abraham's faith reaches further than he could yet see.
ch: The Catechism calls Abraham the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–146) and speaks of the offering of Isaac as the last purifying of his faith: the father of believers is conformed to the Father who did not spare his own Son (CCC 2572). Origen and many Fathers read Isaac carrying the wood as a figure of Christ carrying the Cross (in substance). At Mass the Roman Canon names “the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith”.

set: The day of parables ends as evening falls. Jesus, who has been teaching from the boat, now says, “Let us go across to the other side.” The other side is the country of the Gerasenes (5:1), Gentile land. The Sea of Galilee lies some two hundred metres below sea level, surrounded by hills, and sudden storms are well known there. From here on Mark moves from Jesus' words to his deeds.
str: vv. 35–36: the crossing begins.
vv. 37–38: the storm, Jesus asleep, the disciples' cry.
v. 39: the rebuke and the calm.
vv. 40–41: two questions: Jesus' to them, and theirs to one another.
kw: The same word Jesus used for the unclean spirit in the synagogue (1:25). He speaks to the sea as to an enemy.
Literally “be muzzled”. The same verb Jesus used to the unclean spirit in 1:25.
Three times in the Greek: a great windstorm (v. 37), a great calm (v. 39, “a dead calm”), and a great fear (v. 41, “great awe”). The story moves from the fear of the storm to the fear of God.
vv: But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion; and they woke him up and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”

Only Mark mentions the cushion and has this blunt complaint. Matthew has “Lord, save us!” (8:25). Jesus' sleep is a sign of his trust in the Father (compare Psalm 4:8). The same complaint is found in many prayers.
He woke up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.
In the Old Testament it is God who rules the sea (Psalm 89:9; Job 38:8–11). Psalm 107:29 says of him, “he made the storm be still”. Jesus does what belongs to God.
And they were filled with great awe and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
This is the question of the whole Gospel of Mark. It waits for its answer until the centurion at the Cross (15:39).
ch: Tertullian saw in the boat a figure of the Church, tossed on the sea of this world (On Baptism 12, in substance). St Augustine, preaching on the storm, said that when temptation shakes us it is because Christ is asleep in us, that is, our faith has fallen asleep; so wake him (Sermon 63, in substance). On 27 March 2020, in an empty St Peter's Square during the pandemic, Pope Francis preached on this passage and repeated Jesus' question, “Why are you afraid?”

qa: Why does Jesus reproach the disciples? Is it wrong to cry out to him?
He does not reproach them for praying. The Psalms cry out in just this way. His question is about fear that has forgotten who is in the boat. He first calms the sea, and only then asks the question.
study: When have I, like Abraham, had to set out “not knowing” where I was going? What sustained me?
What storm in my life makes me ask, “Do you not care?” How would I hear Jesus' question there?

lead: Today's question is whose voice to listen to. Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like him, who will speak God's own words. The psalm pleads, “O that today you would listen to his voice!” In the synagogue at Capernaum people hear that voice and are astounded, because Jesus teaches “as one having authority”, and even an unclean spirit has to obey him. The line runs from a promise, through a warning, to its fulfilment. The second reading goes its own way, as it often does on the Sundays of Ordinary Time, when the Lectionary reads St Paul in order rather than choosing a text to match. Yet it also asks about attention, about an undivided heart. The key words are prophet, today, undivided and authority.

set: Deuteronomy presents itself as the farewell addresses of Moses on the plains of Moab, on the edge of the promised land. Israel will soon live among peoples who seek the future through diviners, soothsayers and mediums, and verses 9–14 forbid all of this. How then will Israel know God's will when Moses is gone? This passage is the answer: God himself will provide a prophet.

“Horeb” is Deuteronomy's name for Sinai. Moses recalls the terror of that day, when the people begged not to hear God's voice directly (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:23–27). God approved that request, and so began the office of a mediator of his word.
str: v. 15: the promise: a prophet like Moses, “you shall heed such a prophet”.
v. 16: the origin of the promise: the people's fear at Horeb.
vv. 17–18: God's reply: “I will put my words in the mouth of the prophet”.
v. 19: the duty to listen.
v. 20: the danger of a false prophet.
¶ The verses that follow (vv. 21–22) give a test for telling true prophets from false.
kw: A Hebrew word usually explained as “one called” or “one who calls out”. A prophet is not first a foreteller, but one who speaks for God.
Moses is the measure. The end of the book says plainly that no one like him had yet arisen: “Never since has there arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face” (34:10).

God takes the initiative; a prophet does not appoint himself. In Greek the verb is anistēmi, the same verb the New Testament uses for raising from the dead, and Peter seems to play on it in Acts 3:22, 26.
vv: The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people; you shall heed such a prophet.

“From among your own people”: not a foreign seer, but one of their kin. In its first setting the promise may cover the whole line of true prophets whom God would send to Israel. By the time of Jesus some looked for one particular prophet: the Qumran text 4QTestimonia cites these verses, and John's Gospel shows the question was alive (John 1:21; 6:14).
I will put my words in the mouth of the prophet, who shall speak to them everything that I command.
God says something similar when he calls Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:9). Jesus says of himself that he speaks only what the Father has given him (John 12:49–50).
Anyone who does not heed the words that the prophet shall speak in my name, I myself will hold accountable.
A word from God is never neutral. It has to be answered. Peter quotes the promise in Acts 3:22.
ch: Peter (Acts 3:22) and Stephen (Acts 7:37) apply this promise to Jesus. The Catechism teaches that Christ, the Son of God made man, is the Father's one, perfect and unsurpassable Word, and that there will be no other word than this one (CCC 65). The Second Vatican Council says that Christ completes and perfects Revelation (Dei Verbum 4). The Letter to the Hebrews says it in a sentence: God spoke long ago through the prophets, and in these last days by a Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The Church reads Moses' promise as fulfilled and surpassed, since the prophet like Moses is also the Word himself.

r.h: O that today you would listen
set: Psalm 95 has two halves. It begins as a call to worship and ends with a warning from God's own mouth. For this reason it has long been used to open the daily prayer of the Latin Church, as the Invitatory of the Liturgy of the Hours. Each day the Church begins by hearing this “today”.
str: vv. 1–2: come, let us sing.
vv. 6–7a: come, let us bow down: we are his flock.
vv. 7b–9: the voice changes: “Do not harden your hearts”.
kw: The hinge of the psalm. Hebrews 3:7–4:11 builds a whole sermon on this word: “today” is still open.
The place in the wilderness where the people quarrelled with Moses and put God to the test over water (Exodus 17:1–7). The names themselves tell the story.
vv: O come, let us worship and bow down, let us kneel before the Lord, our Maker!
Three verbs of the body. Worship is not only a thought. In the Latin rite we stand, bow, kneel and strike the breast.
O that today you would listen to his voice!
This links the psalm directly to the first reading: “you shall heed such a prophet”.
Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness,
The hard heart is not the heart that doubts or asks. At Massah the people had already seen God's works and still put him to the test (95:9).
ch: The Catechism says that one word marks the prayer of the Church: “Today!”, echoing the prayer of the Lord and the call of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1165). In the liturgy the saving word of God is not a report about the past. It is addressed to the ones gathered here.

set: Paul writes to Corinth from Ephesus (16:8), usually dated to the mid-50s. In chapter 7 he answers questions the Corinthians have put to him (“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote”, 7:1). He has already defended marriage and the rights of spouses (7:1–16). Now, about the unmarried, he says openly that he has “no command of the Lord” and gives his own opinion (7:25).

Two things must be kept in mind. Paul speaks in the light of “the impending crisis” (7:26) and of the short time ahead (7:29). And he has said at the start that “each has a particular gift from God” (7:7). This Sunday's reading is a pastor's counsel, not a contempt of marriage.
str: v. 32a: the aim: that you may be without anxiety.
vv. 32b–34a: the unmarried man and the married man.
v. 34b: the unmarried woman and the married woman.
v. 35: why he says it: not as a noose, but for good order and devotion.
kw: The word behind “anxieties” in v. 32. It comes from merimnaō, to be anxious or concerned, which Paul then uses for all the people he describes, both married and unmarried. Concern is not a sin; the question is how it is divided.
Literally a noose or halter. Paul has no wish to put a rope around anyone's neck.
“Without being pulled about.” It is related to the word for Martha, who was “distracted” by her many tasks (Luke 10:40). The aim is a heart gathered and attentive.
vv: I want you to be free from anxieties.
The aim is the same for everyone, and it is what Jesus asks in Matthew 6:25–34.
and his interests are divided.
This is a statement of what marriage rightly asks. A husband ought to care how to please his wife. Paul does not call this a sin; he describes it as a real claim on time and heart.
I say this for your own benefit, not to put any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and unhindered devotion to the Lord.
This verse is the key. Every Christian state of life is to serve one end: belonging entirely to the Lord.
ch: The Catechism says that both the sacrament of Matrimony and virginity for the Kingdom of God come from the Lord himself (CCC 1620), and it quotes St John Chrysostom: whoever denigrates marriage also diminishes the glory of virginity. Vatican II calls virginity or celibacy a precious gift of grace by which some give themselves to God alone with an undivided heart, citing this very passage (Lumen Gentium 42). St John Paul II teaches that virginity does not contradict the dignity of marriage but presupposes and confirms it (Familiaris Consortio 16).

set: This is the first public act of Jesus in Mark. He has announced the Kingdom (1:14–15) and called four fishermen (1:16–20). Now, with them, he comes to Capernaum, a town on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee which becomes the centre of his work in Galilee.
